paragraphs.text: PREFACE.
Nothing held within the framework of the world is immortal:
not the earth, not the kingdoms of men, not golden Rome,
not the sea, not the land, not the fiery stars of heaven.
For the Father of all things has fixed a time that cannot be revoked,
when the last flame will sweep away the whole world in its blaze.
Yet lofty deeds and the honor of virtue
keep countless men alive in memory for long ages,
and poets heap up their fame and praises.
Some are celebrated by the lofty songs that flow from the spring of Smyrna,
others by the sweetness of Maro, son of the Mincius.
Nor is the glory of the poets themselves any less widespread;
it endures almost like something eternal, as long as the ages fly on
and the turning of the heavens wheels the starry sky
around the lands and seas under its appointed governance.
But if songs have earned such lasting fame
that weave falsehoods into the deeds of men of old,
then for me the sure truth of a praise eternal through the ages
will grant immortal glory and pay back what I have earned.
For my song shall be the life-giving deeds of Christ, [?]
a divine gift to the nations, free from the guilt of falsehood.
Nor do I fear that the fires of the world will sweep away
this work along with it; for perhaps this work will rescue me from the fire
on that day when, flashing from a flame-spewing cloud, there will descend
the Judge, the glory of the high-throned Father, Christ.
Come then! May the Holy Spirit, the author of my song, be with me,
and may the sweet Jordan water the singer's mind with its pure stream,
so that we may speak words worthy of Christ.
BOOK ONE.
Herod was king, a bloodthirsty king, among the Jewish people,
and under him lived a guardian of justice, a priest of the temple,
Zechariah, whose task it was to keep watch over the temple in his turn,
as the appointed order of the chosen priests came round.
Joined to him in marriage was a most worthy wife.
Both shared the same care for just and upright conduct;
the precepts of the law held them both, bound together.
They had no children, and their years were already declining,
so that the gift might be all the more welcome to those who had given up hope.
But when Zechariah happened to be offering incense in the sanctuary at the altar,
a messenger appeared, coming down from the opened heaven,
to deliver the words he had been commanded to him alone
(for the rest of the people were then praying, prostrate at the doors):
"What fear has this terrible sight struck into your heart,
when the grace of a joyful message should set you at peace?
For the one Father of all things has sent me from the lofty
throne of heaven and commands me now to come and speak with you,
and he promises that soon a son will be born to you from your dear wife,
for whom great glory in the world lies in store,
who by his birth will bring great joy to the peoples;
sober for ever, he whom the Spirit, while he is still enclosed in his mother's very
womb, will fill with shining divine power.
By his teaching he will turn the greater part of this people
to the true way, and he will be the first to recognize
at once his Lord and God, and he will renew the people.
Remember to call him by the name John."
The priest answered him with troubled mind:
"Age stands against such promises as their rival,
nor can offspring come to the old and weary,
when God turned away and denied it in the first flower of our youth."
So spoke the trembling priest; and the messenger added these words:
"If some mortal had promised you offspring,
then perhaps your mind's hesitation might well have
clung to slow words and leaned toward despair.
But now I, whom the Lord of heaven, the maker of the earth,
willed to stand as a minister before his face,
have been received by a man's ungrateful ears and eyes,
and have delivered the commands of the supreme God only to have them scorned.
Therefore the gift remains irrevocable, as promised,
but your voice, the messenger of your swift mind, will be shut off,
until all God's gifts have been made sure to you both."
So he spoke, and melted into the thin air.
Meanwhile the people were left long in wonder
at why the priest should linger so long in the temple.
Coming out, trembling, he showed them by gestures that he had seen a heavenly power,
and that he had suffered the wretched loss of his voice.
Then, having completed his service in its due order, the priest returns home,
and the promises lighten the loss of his speech;
nor was the gift of offspring long delayed.
But his wife anxiously concealed the joy of her womb
until the moon had filled out its hollow crescent five times.
Then the same minister brought still greater commands,
sent to the ears of the virgin Mary.
She had been betrothed to her kinsman for a fixed time,
to grow to womanhood chastely, hidden within a maiden's dwelling,
and was permitted by her parents' command to await the appointed day.
To her the messenger began in calm words:
"Hail, you who will help the earth with saving offspring;
do not let this awe-inspiring sight trouble your mind.
For by heaven's command your womb will conceive
a son, whom God both rejoices and commands to reign through all ages
and to be believed his own offspring.
When you have brought him into the light, let his name be Jesus."
Then the virgin began to answer him with frightened lips:
"They say no child is conceived without a husband;
from where, then, shall I hope that offspring will come to me?"
The messenger replied to this in swift words:
"The lofty power of God will hover around you, overshadowing you,
and the pure Spirit will come, most chosen virgin,
and soon with a chaste word will command that a boy be born to you,
glorious for the peoples, whom all must believe holy
and call the Son of the most high God.
So too your kinswoman, whom everyone believed barren,
the wife of Zechariah, has lately, from mortal seed,
received a wonder into limbs worn out with age.
This is her sixth month: so all things obey his commands."
Then the virgin: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord, who commands;
as your words declare, you see her ready to serve."
The messenger departed and vanished into the empty air.
Then with swift steps she made her way to a city of Judea
and entered Zechariah's house, and greeted the pregnant
Elizabeth, whereupon at once the restless limbs of the child enclosed
in her womb leapt up with a stronger movement.
And at the same moment the mother sprang up, shaken with trembling,
and was filled with the holy breath of the divine voice,
and cried aloud: "O blessed woman, hail,
you who carry a blessed child in the curve of your womb.
Why has just God willed to make my house
illustrious with such honor, that the mother of the most high God
should visit it? See, the child in my womb
leaps for joy, as soon as it heard Mary's first greeting.
Blessed is she who believes that fulfillment will soon come to the words
which great God, in his condescension, will speak to his servants."
She, her spirit carried along by joy mingled with modesty,
poured out trembling words in a hushed voice:
"My soul returns magnificent praise and thanks
to the Lord of the boundless world. This spirit of mine can scarcely
contain such joys, because just God has deigned to raise me
on high from lowliness, and has willed that I be held exalted and blessed
by all nations and all ages.
See, he has taken away the throne from the cruel and broken the proud,
and enriched the humble and needy with overflowing wealth."
Then she stayed there three months in succession,
and returned to her own home, now sure of what was to come.
And now the time had come when the turning days
would compel Elizabeth to bring forth the promised child
into the shores of light. At the news of the birth a crowd
of kinsfolk came running, and thronging together they celebrated wondrous joys
and insisted that he should have his father's name.
His mother refused this, and repeated again and again that he should be called John.
Then they decided to consult the wishes of the mute father,
and asked him to declare the name in writing.
But—O wondrous faith!—when he tries to write on the tablets,
his tied tongue is loosed into sounding words.
Soon inspiration also enters his familiar mind,
and, filled with it, he sings words that know the future:
"Let all join in celebrating praises and give thanks again and again
to the Father of the stars and earth, of the sea and of men,
because he has willed to visit his own people and set them free.
See, he blesses an ancient race, and raising up a horn of salvation
grants a light from the line of David.
This is what the prophets of old sang, one after another;
this is that salvation by which he snatches us from dark enemies,
so that we may serve the Just One justly.
And you, little child, will be called a holy and worthy prophet,
and soon you will go before the Lord on his way
and lead his people through the open light:
through you they will spurn error, and the darkness of death
will be broken through by all who follow your precepts."
From then on the boy's life was spent always hidden
in remote valleys, until, as the years required,
he grew to full age for the office of a prophet.
Meanwhile wonder troubled the mind of Mary's betrothed,
because he saw the evident burden of her womb,
and he pondered within himself how he might conceal
his kinswoman's hidden disgrace and refuse the marriage.
As he turned these things over, his limbs grew heavy with sleep,
and above his fearful dreams he heard the voice of God:
"Take in marriage your betrothed, who is guilty of no crime,
whose womb the Spirit has filled with a holy child.
Of her the prophet sang that she would come, and of a child born from a virgin,
whose name is GOD WITH US." At once he,
following these commands, kept the pledge of betrothal.
But it happened then that a reckoning of heads in a new census,
by order of Caesar Augustus, was being recorded
across most of the world; at that time Syria was lawfully governed
by Quirinius, to whom, throughout all the towns, the peoples
declared their own properties, their means, their names and lineage.
There is a city of Judea, Bethlehem, which gave birth to David the singer,
and which by right required the registration of his descendants.
Here Joseph, of the line of David, registered Mary,
recording her as betrothed to him and declaring her with child.
For lodging for the two of them, beneath the walls of the city of Bethlehem,
there was only a tiny dwelling in the cramped countryside.
There the virgin, her time fulfilled with the new child,
was delivered, and swaddling clothes of old cloth
wrapped the boy, and a hard manger was given him for a bed.
Nearby, the anxious watch over their flocks by night
kept shepherds awake across the rich pastures.
Behold, at God's bidding a messenger was seen coming down from heaven,
and sudden terror, shaking them with fear,
threw the shepherds' bodies prostrate on the green earth.
And a voice sent from heaven came swiftly to the astonished men:
"Put away the terror in your minds and receive my words,
shepherds, to whom I bring these great joys.
For a boy has been born of the famous line of David,
who will soon spread light and gladness to the peoples.
This sign I will tell you: you may now see the boy
filling the manger with his small voice."
As he spoke, thousands of the heavenly host joined him,
and all of them praised God and called upon him,
and the voice of the united host filled the air with these words:
"Due glory attends the supreme Father;
on earth a fitting peace will follow just men."
And with these words they returned to the hidden places of heaven.
The shepherds came quickly and saw the boy lying
in the lap of the manger; and afterward, in great numbers,
they scattered far and wide the roving seeds of swift report.
Wondering, they gave praise; rejoicing, they were astounded
that everything had turned out true to the warnings of the night.
The boy had seen the eighth day: now he must be circumcised
according to the custom of the law, and given a name.
And the name given him was the one that once, by heavenly instruction,
the voice sent from God had commanded to Mary: Jesus.
Moses had written down the rules of the ancient law,
among which he ordered the descendants of the ancient blood of the patriarchs
to observe the offering of their firstborn to be consecrated,
and to bring unfledged doves to the shrine as well.
When these rites were being kept by Mary in the temple,
behold, old Simeon, worthy to grasp with his understanding
the voices of heaven, to whom long before a power that foreknew
what was to come had revealed that he would lay aside the prison of his sick body
and see death and rest, set free,
as soon as he had seen the praise of heaven and the salvation of earth,
the Christ whom all the oracles of the prophets promise,
brought to the temple with the customary doves.
And when, weary and bent in body, he made his way
heavily into the temple, as the Spirit, his guide, had prompted him,
behold, at that very moment he perceived that little Jesus, in his mother's lap,
had come to the temple; with trembling arms
he took the boy, and joyfully spoke these words:
"Now, now, Lord, now you set me, your servant, free from the dark
chains of the body, and deign to bring your words to fulfillment
with peace for your own. See, your splendid light
surrounds our eyes and shines with its rays,
the light which, having illumined all the nations of men,
is added as the crowning glory of the people of Israel.
Why is the heart of Mary, his mother, so astonished?
This boy is given for the fall of the people; he will grant
the peoples to be born again; he will become a sign
spoken against, and a sword will pass through what is owed to death
and through his mother's soul with gleaming steel,
so that the dark folds of hidden hearts may be laid open."
So God spoke in Simeon; and soon he filled a woman's mind
with the holy breath of prophecy.
Anna was far advanced in years; in the flower of her youth
her husband's untimely death had left her a widow.
But in place of a husband a chaste life in the temple
and the worship of God were ever her portion; at divine command she
recognized the Christ and spoke in similar words.
Then, when his mother had fulfilled the solemn law for the boy's name,
together with Joseph, who marveled at everything,
they joyfully returned to their homeland and carried the boy back.
There is a people far off, familiar with the rising sun,
skilled in marking the risings and settings of the stars;
their leading men bore the name of Magi.
Then chosen men from there, by long roads, arrive in Jerusalem,
approach the king, and ask to be told
in what region Judea, under his rule, held a boy
newly born: they had been prompted by the rising of a shining star
to make the journey, so that with suppliant hands
they might worship the venerable Godhead risen upon the earth.
Herod, terrified, summoned by his command the chief priests of Jerusalem
and those who study the predictions of the ancient prophets,
and ordered them to search the whole of the law
to make plain which walls were to be the birthplace of Christ,
whose coming all the oracles of the prophets promise.
Then it was made clear that he was destined to be born
within the walls of Bethlehem, he who must lead the sacred people
of the Israelites by holy power.
Herod then ordered the Persians to continue on their way
and, when they found the boy, to show him to Herod, that he too might worship him.
Behold, midway on their journey they see a star going before them,
furrowing the air with flames, which stopped at the very top
and lit up and showed the dwelling of the boy.
The Magi rejoiced with great joy and hailed the star,
and when they saw the boy at his mother's breast,
they cast themselves down, lying prostrate on the ground,
and humbly made their supplication; then three gifts,
incense, gold, and myrrh, to the king, the man, and the God,
they offered. Soon fearful dreams troubled them all night long
and bade them avoid the cruel tyrant.
And so by other paths they fled Herod's court,
and the Magi returned secretly to their homeland.
Joseph, too, driven by heavenly warnings,
carried the boy away with his mother into Egypt.
But savage Herod believed that one would succeed him
whom the care of the Magi, skilled in the stars, had sought out.
Troubled by their cautious departure,
he ordered a horrible slaughter through the streets of Bethlehem.
All the infants, the tender folk still at the breast,
he tore away with the sword, though they were guilty of no crime.
This slaughter too had long stood foretold,
which good Jeremiah, commanded by divine power,
laments: mothers, over the wretched death of their children,
beating heavily on heaven with dreadful cries.
But when his fury had died down and the cruel savagery of the tyrant
had been sated with the horrible blood of infants,
he thought he had destroyed all the poor little ones who had reached
one or two years of their doomed life.
Again, his limbs held fast by a wondrous sleep,
Joseph was urged by warnings to bring Mary and the boy
from Egypt to their homeland, where happy Nazareth
gave the boy the name foretold long ago.
And once the foretelling voice of another prophet,
inspired by God, had said: "He will come, my offspring will come
out of deep Egypt, light and salvation for the earth."
The child grew with the swift steps of the years;
his wisdom outran his age and went before it,
and venerable grace shone in his face and in his words.
And now he had reached twice six years of age,
when his parents, keeping the rite of Passover according to custom,
used to bring the boy to the temple for the joyful feast
at every turning of the year, as was their custom.
So they were there together for Passover, and when all the days
of the feast were completed they were preparing to return home,
when the boy, amid the crowd, left the footsteps of the mother
he was accompanying, and gladly sought the inner places of the temple.
Through the streets of the city and through hidden houses,
along the roads of the journey, among acquaintances and kinsfolk,
his mother searched for him; but when the third day came,
she hurried back to the temple, and found him seated among
the companies of the teachers, discussing the obscurities of the laws
with the assembly of elders. The elders could scarcely find wonder enough
for the boy's words; but his loving mother
said: "Son, I have been searching for you, lost, with flowing tears,
anxious and grieving along with your father. What reason
parts you from your parents' path and keeps you here in the house of the temple?"
But he said: "Why do you look for me so, why do you look for me?
Do you not yet understand, mother, that by right the son
must dwell in his Father's seat and house?"
So he spoke, and joined them on the road and went back home;
nor did his mother grasp the weight of so great a word,
yet they kept all these things in order in the secret of their hearts.
And the boy, with fitting and most gentle obedience,
always bound them both closely in love to himself.
Meanwhile the sequence of the ages, running through all that the ancient scripture had pledged,
was drawing all the promises toward fulfillment.
The son of Zechariah, in the desert valleys, was calling everyone
with a loud cry to lay aside their stains,
so that they might receive the wondrous washing of the clear river,
by which the soul's virtue might shine, its filth washed away,
as the prophet Isaiah, at divine command, had sung:
"A voice resounds far and wide through the desert valleys: build
broad highways, let every path of the roads be straight,
fit to bear worthily the footsteps of the Lord.
The hills will sink down, every valley will be filled;
the good line of a straight road will set the windings right,
and to see with bodily eyes the serene light
the Father and Lord of salvation grants to all."
So the peoples came, rushing in from every side,
crowding the banks and eagerly seeking the washing.
The prophet's garments were woven from camels' hair,
and a belt of hide girded his waist,
and wild honey provided his meager food.
And when he saw so many peoples, come from different places,
rushing to the river, he began to speak thus:
"Offspring of a brood of vipers, who has shown you how to escape
the punishments you deserve and the wrath that presses upon you?
But, wretched ones, if you repent, bear fitting fruit,
and let no confidence in your descent make your minds proud.
For easily, even from stones, a people will arise
to take your name, since you, a degenerate offspring, go astray.
Already, already, close against the oaken roots,
before the eyes of all, stands the lifted blade of the axe.
The barren forests will be cut down and will feed the fire.
Now I have undertaken to wash away past stains
in the pure river; but another will come, stronger than I,
the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to touch.
He will wash the mind of man with the Holy Spirit
and purge guilty hearts with balls of flame.
In his hands, too, the farmer's winnowing shovel is held,
and his own threshing floor of grain will be cleansed,
and an abundance of sifted wheat will fill the barns,
and eternal fire will consume the light chaff."
So he spoke, and he saw Him coming with hurried steps through the wood,
seeking the venerable washing of the Jordan.
But the prophet protested, forbidding him, and spoke thus:
"Do you deign to be plunged into the waters by my hands,
when your washing could cleanse me far better?"
So spoke John, and Jesus answered him thus:
"Allow it now, for this is fitting; so in all things
the holy order of righteousness that we must pursue will be fulfilled."
With these words he entered the glassy waters of the river.
As he rose, the manifest presence of God shone out.
The golden ether of the sevenfold heaven was split open,
and, taking bodily form, there came down from on high
the Spirit, in the likeness of a dove of the air, out of a cloud,
and poured holy breath over the body of Jesus.
Then a voice sent from God sped through the long void
and addressed Christ, washed in the waters and anointed with the breath:
"You, Son, I joyfully declare today
to be begotten of me; this glory of my offspring pleases me."
Then he sought the shady mountains and the lairs of wild beasts,
and the Father's ministers were swiftly vying to offer him service;
soon envy seized the demon's black mind
with terror, and the sick one did not lack, meanwhile,
the deceitful cunning to tempt Christ.
Forty suns in succession had passed for him
since he had taken any nourishment of food or drink;
rather, the unbroken fasting of a steadfast heart
kept the hidden depths of his mind turned toward the kingdom of the world.
Then at last his body warned him to seek food.
Meanwhile the deceit of dreadful wickedness tempted him:
"If God has truly begotten you," it said, "you will be able
with a strong word to command all these stones
to take on the use and form of wheaten bread."
Christ replied to this: "Such things do not trouble me now;
for I remember it is written that the ready substance of bread
will not by itself sustain the life of the believer,
but power fills devout hearts through the word of God."
But again the tempter, fitting his snares with crafty arts,
hastened to weave them. For when it saw that he was soon to set foot
within the walls of the city, the livid power made Christ
stand on the marble summit of the temple.
Then it attacked him thus, with the deceiving poison of its voice:
"If God is truly your father, from the summit of the temple
you will hurl your body with a leap through the empty air.
Scripture will be your witness, which openly promises
that the supreme Father has given such a command to his ministers,
that they should take care to protect a body in its fall;
and they will hasten to lift your limbs with serving hands,
so that no stone may strike and injure the soles of your feet."
Christ answered these words with words of his own:
"I must rather remember the heavenly scripture,
that confident boldness must not put the powers of the Lord to the test."
Again, soon after, the raging deceiver made Christ stand
on the lofty ridges of a steep mountain,
showing him the shining kingdoms throughout the world:
"Do you see," it said, "how great is the glory of all these things?
All of them I can give to your rule right now,
if you will honor me and worship me, who grant such gifts."
Then Jesus repelled it as it pressed him with these words:
"Begone, mad frenzy of pestilent poison,
for the command stands fixed and immovable for us for ever,
that the just man should devoutly worship the Lord of heaven
and, serving him, revere the name of the One for ever."
Driven off by such words, the demon fled through trackless ways.
When he learned that John had been thrust into the shadows
of prison, he held the grief down in his sorrowful heart,
and decided to make his home in the territory of Zebulun,
so that the saying of Isaiah might be fulfilled after its long course:
"Land of Zebulun and the region that bears the name of Naphtali,
and the way beyond the sea, far across the fields of Galilee,
and beyond the Jordan, nations and peoples shut in darkness
will see a great and sudden light,
and for those who sit in the shadow of death a kindly
will of faith rises up, shining with light."
So Christ announced that the gifts of the reigning God were at hand,
rebuking them, and making a full proclamation of salvation.
And passing along the seashore he saw two brothers,
rock-solid Simon, worthy of the surname Peter,
and Andrew with him, setting the curving folds of their linen nets
as traps for fish in the waters of the sea.
"Now," he said, "you catch fish in the deep swell of the sea,
but if you are willing to follow me, rich
and most beautiful gains will come to you from the hunting of men."
At once, sure and steadfast of heart,
they threw down their nets and together followed his command.
After these brothers, when he saw James and John
weaving snares of meshed fabric for the flocks of the sea,
and gave them the same call from the shore,
they left their father Zebedee in the boat,
following at once the most beautiful commands of salvation.
From then on, throughout the land of Galilee, Christ sowed
the holy proclamation of the kingdom, instilling it in the peoples,
and gave swift healing to the weak and the sick;
and soon a widespread report had already filled distant Syria,
telling in a thousand words of Christ's present gifts.
At last, vying with one another, they brought to Christ those wasted by the decay of illness
and bound by various ills, whose bodily strength a long
wasting disease had ravaged and consumed with pain;
and with an effortless gift
he quickly restored them all, made whole, to wondrous joy.
And now the diseases of the soul itself, and savage frenzies,
and the madness of mind that follows the course of the moon
departed, commanded by the weighty power of his word.
As he worked great miracles, mixed crowds thronged around him
and followed him, people of Jerusalem and of Syria,
and populous Judea, and the folk of Galilee,
and those whom the Jordan divides with its still stream.
Seeing these peoples, he sat down on a very high rock,
and with his disciples gathered close around him he began thus:
"Blessed are the humble, whom a poor spirit surrounds,
for the lofty kingdom of heaven receives them;
like them are the meek, whom gentleness crowns,
to whose possession the most beautiful earth is owed.
In the same way great consolation will come to those who mourn.
Those who now seek the food and drink of righteousness
will find a full and abundant table awaiting to satisfy them.
Blessed is he who has grieved from his heart over the lot of the wretched,
for the Lord's abundant mercy will await him.
Blessed are those who look upon heaven with a pure heart;
God, made visible, will be revealed to them through all ages.
The peacemakers God adopts into the number of his children.
Happy beyond measure are those whom gnashing persecution
oppresses for righteousness' sake; to them the kingdom of heaven will soon
be opened. Rejoice, you who hold fast to righteous works,
whom headlong injustice will drive with cruel goads;
for a very great reward is kept for you in the heavens,
since such was the persecution of the prophets.
Learn that you are the savor of salt upon this earth.
If this savor loses its strength and now grows stale,
what substance of salt will sharpen the taste that is spent?
After that no use is left for worthless salt
except to be thrown far away and trampled by every foot.
You are the bright light of the world: do not hide it.
For who could hide a city set upon lofty crags?
So let your light reach
all people, and let the beauty of your deeds be set
in the clear light. Let all people praise the glory
of your Father, whose throne is the palace of high heaven.
I have not come now to abolish the ancient laws,
nor to overturn the commands the prophets of old laid down;
for all of them will be fulfilled for you through me.
I tell you the truth: until heaven and earth and sea
come to their end, not even a letter of the law
or the slender stroke of the smallest mark will be lacking;
rather, all will come to pass in the ordered course of the ages.
For if anyone dares to loosen the least part
of a commandment, and by his daring teaches others to do the same,
he will be called least in the heavenly seat.
But whoever keeps the rule in his own conduct
and at the same time hands on the forefathers' precepts unbroken
will be great and will bear a great name beyond the stars.
You have heard the command given under the rule of the old law:
if anyone stains his hands with human blood,
he is guilty and will pay the penalty to the avenging sword.
But I command that no one dare to rise up in anger
or be stirred by seething hatred for his brother.
Such a man is guilty and will pay the penalty before a just judge.
And no lesser flame will follow the insults of those
who call their brother a fool or a wretch.
If, revering the altar, you wish to offer a gift,
and it then comes into the inner depths of your silent mind
that a quarrel has arisen at home between you and your brother,
leave all your gifts there, brought up to the sanctuary,
and first hurry off to seek peace.
Then, once you have been reconciled in brotherly love,
offer God welcome gifts with a calm heart.
The power of the body, moreover, is always your adversary;
let it be tended quickly with chaste love
while it walks with you along the crossroads of swift life.
For the use of a polluted body will accuse you
and set you in chains before the judge on high.
Once you are condemned, his officers will drag you to cruel chains,
and you will not be released from the darkness of the black prison
until the last part of the smallest coin is paid.
The warning of the law is not unknown to you, I think,
which forbids the body adultery; but now my commands
curb the hidden strivings of the inner mind:
the penalty must be paid for what is desired no less than for what is done.
If the straying of your right eye should ensnare you,
hurry to tear out the source of the wretched stain
and fling it far away. For it is better to lose
a small member than to hand the whole body over to the flames
and entangle the soul along with it in everlasting punishment.
And if your right hand leads your mind down wayward paths,
it is better to cut off the cause of error with the blade
than to give the whole body over to eternal flames.
The ancients instruct that if anyone breaks off a marriage,
he must write a bill of divorce, the deadly words of the law.
Only an adulteress may rightly leave her husband's house;
let other wives remain, for the rights of chaste modesty
are lost by a wife whose husband has deserted her, and he is the cause.
The ancient laws forbid the tongue to swear falsely,
but let boldness in swearing give way to our commands.
It is not right for anyone to swear by high heaven,
for it is the Lord's seat; nor shall anyone ever swear by the earth,
which bears the footprints of God, or by the venerable name of Jerusalem,
for that city belongs to the great King.
Nor will anyone be permitted to swear by his own head,
for you see that you have no power over even the smallest hair
to change its color to white or to black.
[?] Let "It is, it is" be enough; and what is not, say: "It is not."
Whatever goes beyond these words is all slyly
suggested to the sick mind by the foul, creeping power of poison.
You have long held the well-known precepts of the law:
let like vengeance always follow the one who does harm;
but calm patience will overcome evil better.
And if anyone strikes one side of your face with his palm,
remember to offer him the other side at once.
Or if anyone, pressing his case by force of a judge, takes your tunic,
give it up willingly, and let him take your cloak along with it.
If someone should order you to go a mile's road
and bear the toil of a heavy load,
go at once, and go with him twice the distance.
If anyone in need asks of you, or even pretends to be in need,
give generously out of heartfelt pity; and if anyone begs
a loan, grant it, and do not turn your kind face away.
Do not be content to help only your friends
or, with blind hatred, to think your enemies deserve hatred.
Rather, I command you always to show gentle kindness to all
and to move God with kindly prayers
for the life of those who delight in destroying you
and pursue you fiercely with hostile minds and hatred.
For our Father has given the sun's light to all alike
and has given the rains alike to the just and the wicked.
But if we honor only the friends close to us,
what room can there be here for a just reward?
Even a people devoted to profit serves friendship in that way.
But you must be like your perfect Father.
Whenever a fair opportunity to do right presents itself,
avoid the eyes of men; for no reward will remain
to follow such a deed afterward;
only the barren praise of the crowd will applaud it.
Rather, let the right hand do what it does; it will be fitting
for the left hand not to know it; then the only searcher of the hidden heart
will repay rewards worthy of just merits.
There are some whom the boasting of a swollen mind puffs up;
they rejoice to have crowds standing by as they pray,
and they wear out the day spinning out floods of words;
the only fruit of such prayers is empty display.
But let the secret inner rooms of the house be closed
for chaste prayers, and you shall worship God in few words.
The Father himself knows what anxiety troubles your heart.
We say nothing without God present; the hidden caverns
of the closed heart conceal nothing; God is present and sees all.
So let it be your pleasure to make your prayer in these words:
"Father, dwelling on the starry summit of heaven,
may the reverence of your name, we pray, be hallowed
in us, Father on high; may your kingdom come
in peace upon the world, and may kindly light reveal it.
As in heaven, so on earth may your glorious will be done;
and today may the life-giving substance of holy bread
come to us; may your bounty soon, in its indulgence,
release the countless debts of wicked error,
and may we in just the same way forgive what our debtors owe us.
May the cruel temptation of the foul demon be far from us,
and may your right hand lift us out of evils into the light."
For the Father will forgive the peoples their offenses
on this condition: if you are willing to pardon one another's sins
and do not set a hard heart against wrongs done to you.
The fasts of the people are also most pleasing to God;
but many take pains to disfigure their own faces,
so that their fasting may win them empty fame among men.
But you, with your hair made glossy with pleasant olive oil,
wash your cheerful face in pure spring water,
so that the Father alone, seeing the deep service
of a devoted heart, may praise it and repay its merit.
It is vain to keep watch over talents buried in the ground.
There rust and devouring moths hold sway,
and thieves dig everything out of its hiding place and plunder it.
Store up treasures for yourselves on the summit of heaven;
neither rust nor moths nor the dreadful gang of thieves
will plunder them there. Where your wealth is stored,
there your hearts too are held under the same sway.
The body has a light by which you see the light all share;
if the eye's gaze shines pure and single,
the limbs of the whole body will shine brightly.
But if it is wicked and sees but little,
dark shadows will lie heavy on all the members.
And if the light is turned into black shadows,
how great will be the horror of the darkness itself without light?
No one can serve two masters equally;
he will give way either to hatred of one or to love of him,
and no servant will put up with both masters alike.
No one will ever be able to serve riches and God
at the same time; but keep these commands:
do not let clothing for your body trouble you,
and do not seek after easy food with anxious care.
Do we not value life more than the body's food?
Or does anyone hesitate to put the body before clothing?
Let us look at the birds of the air: do they press the plowshare
and break the back of the soil, or sow seeds of grain,
or cut the stalks of the crops with the curved sickle?
Yet plenty of food and drink comes to them.
Does God not care far more about human beings?
Nor was it fitting to hang anxiety about clothing
upon our hearts; no, not even if men could add
a cubit's growth to their own limbs.
See how the lilies gleam across the rich fields!
Yet no labor has ever burdened them,
and not even the famous Solomon, when the court of his rich kingdom
overflowed with wealth, was clothed in such graceful garments.
But if God himself clothes the glad greenery of meadows and shrubs,
which is destined for our fires,
why do you not put greater trust in the Father?
So food, drink, clothing, and all empty things —
leave this earthly care to the faithless nations.
Rather, seek as is fitting the heavenly kingdom
and the righteousness of God — all else will come of its own accord —
and do not trouble yourselves over tomorrow's supply of goods;
each day is enough for itself, with its own day's trouble.
Let cruel condemnation have no part in your judgment;
for the Lord will follow the precedents of your own law,
which you lay down on earth while you are held by time:
you must bear the very measure that you set.
You see the speck clinging in your brother's eye,
yet do not notice the beam lodged in your own,
and you labor to cleanse another's eye first;
but tear the deceiving timber out of your own eye,
and then take care to remove the other's tiny splinter.
Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not
shamefully throw necklaces before unclean swine.
For they will lie trampled underfoot in the mud,
and the swine will turn and tear you with gaping wounds.
Whoever asks will be given; whoever seeks will find and keep;
and to whoever knocks, the doors will open and let him in.
None of you men, when your children ask for bread,
will give them a stone, or a snake when they ask for fish;
you, I say, hard as you are, with hardness rooted
deep in your hearts, will always give good things to your children.
How much more does the indulgent Father of mankind
rejoice to grant gentle good things, as is fitting, to those who ask rightly!
The kindnesses you wish men would show to you,
show those same kindnesses to all out of your goodwill.
This is the sum of the law; this is the rule the prophets declared.
Go, you righteous, through the narrow gate above the sky.
How broad and spacious is the road that, on the left-hand path,
winds its steep way down into the darkness of death,
and countless crowds go down its slope!
The path of life is hemmed in by huge rocks,
and lofty virtue leads scarcely a few across the rugged ground.
But if the deceitful and enticing plain of evil,
slippery with its ugly falls, has too strongly beguiled any,
it seizes them and drags them headlong, like a rushing river,
or a spirited horse running unbridled with its reins broken,
or a ship without a helmsman on windswept seas.
Beware of those who under a false name
lay traps for you and are called prophets.
They are clothed in the likeness of sheep, but beneath their fraud
they hide the savage hearts of wolves, and they drag off and tear apart
the unwary flocks of those who give way, deceived by cruel error.
Such monsters are known by their own fruits;
you must see what end their deceitful teaching aims at.
For you have never seen figs growing from thistles
or grapes from brambles anywhere across the countryside.
And as a tree is clothed with the growth of its own fruit,
so their deceit is laid bare when the fruit reveals it.
I will not be moved by the words and honors of flatterers,
and they will not win the rewards of the heavenly seat as a matter of course
merely because fawning flattery calls me Lord.
Rather, those will rightly rejoice in the gift of the kingdom
who willingly do the commands of our Father.
Soon the final day will come, which with stern justice
will grant rewards to righteousness and Gehenna to crime.
Then many will cry out to me with weeping, saying:
"Did not mighty powers once, in your name,
subdue all things for us at our holy commands?
Often too our voice was counted among the prophets,
and demons served us in your name."
Then I will swear to them that I have never known
such a life of men, which is foul with wicked deeds.
Whoever devotes both ears and deeds to my teachings,
I will liken him to a man laying foundations on solid rock,
on which walls rise well balanced.
That house will stand unharmed by rain and wind
and by its firm strength will overcome the threats of torrents,
because its foundations cling to immovable rock.
But whoever holds my commands only by hearing them
and goes far off on slippery paths with contrary deeds,
I will make him like one who props the foundations
of his house on shifting sand; at the first blast of wind
and when the rain begins to beat down in pouring streams,
the whole structure collapses as its weight gives way,
and ruin follows with the heavy wreck of the roof."
As he said these things, the people stood fixed in wonder,
astonished beyond measure, for the authority granted to Christ
had risen far above the teaching of the ancients.
Then, as he left the heights of the lofty mountain,
a joyful crowd of people pressed around him as they followed.
But look: a young man, pierced to the vitals by dreadful decay,
whose whole body leprosy had besieged and disfigured,
fell down in reverence and begged Christ:
"For me to be rid at last of the weight of so great a sickness,
your willing it will be enough." Then the right hand of Christ
by its touch alone cleansed the ghastly limbs.
And to the man, now healed, he gave the command: "Hide your joy,
and in obedience to the law offer your gifts at the temple."
As he went on from there, a centurion at once came to him
as a suppliant and, throwing himself down, pleaded with these words:
"The spirit of a young boy is tormented with sickness;
a sudden illness has undone every function of his limbs,
and now only pain, outliving them, keeps hold of life.
But have mercy by a command, I beg you; for our sins forbid
the Father of life and light to come under our roof.
It is enough now that by a word you order health to return.
For my own authority has often in this way compelled the men
under me to obey by a word the duties I commanded."
So he spoke. Moved by the man's prayers and faith,
Jesus turned and spoke these words to the people following him:
"Never do I remember finding such faith
in our ancestral nation; but learn from these true words
that the lofty kingdom of heaven will call many people
born in different parts of the world
to recline with our fathers at the table of life,
while the fathers' own offspring, plunged into blind darkness,
gnashing their teeth horribly and weeping without end,
will be driven to undergo the everlasting torments of punishment.
But to you, young man, faithful in strength of mind,
the fruit will come as you believe, with the light of health."
So he spoke, and quicker than speech, together with the speaker's voice,
the gifts of his swift word sped across to the boy;
and the soldier, hurrying back and entering his house,
rejoiced that the gifts of God the healer had arrived before him.
From there holy Jesus went into the house of Peter,
whose mother-in-law lay gasping with burning fever.
And as Jesus the Savior touched her right hand,
the woman, healed, served at the table.
BOOK TWO.
And now the day, departing with its sinking light,
had fallen into the sea, and dark-blue night was drawing her dusky mantle,
embroidered with starry flames, across the void,
when many people, collapsing in sickness of mind
and bound in soul by the raging craft of a demon,
were carried to him by crowds who vied with one another in the now-blind night.
But the Word of Christ removed that great sickness
and, kind to all, bestowed the Father's gifts.
But lo, when the light had risen, a greater tumult arose
with throngs of grateful people; troubled, he
ordered his disciples to launch the tall ship
into the sail-winged sea. Then a scribe, pouring out prayers,
asked to go away with the Holy One in the boat as well.
Christ said to him: 'Where will you follow me, scribe?
For foxes the rock hollowed out in the woodland
provides lairs, and the forest gives rest to the birds of the air;
but the Son of Man is permitted to come under no roof:
such are the schemes of your nation.'
Then one of the disciples asked in these words:
'The last rites are owed to my dead father,
but may your will, Holy One, grant us time
to bury the body of my poor father.'
Christ replied: 'Better that you go along on our journey
and leave the dead to bury the dead in the earth.'
They board the ship, and, filled with a fitting wind,
the sails swell, and the keel flies over the hissing wave.
After the ship had reached the deep, the sea began to rise
in wrath and to swell with winds let loose from either side
and to heave raging mountains up toward the sky;
now it strikes the stern with its mass, now the prow with a whirlwind,
and the planks of the sides take in the waves that dash over them,
and as the deep is torn apart, the very ground lies bare.
Meanwhile Jesus was sleeping in the stern.
The disciples and sailors alike, in fear,
beg him to wake up and show him the perils of the sea.
Then he said: 'How little faith there is in you!
Fear rushes into faithless hearts!' Then he commands
the storms and spreads a calm peace over the waters.
They mingle their wonder in fearful talk
among themselves: what great power had been granted him,
or what command this is, to which the straits stirred up by the winds
and the storms, rearing up with threats, bow their necks.
Now the ship had come to rest beneath the shore of the Gerasenes;
but lo, as he disembarked, a young man—wonderful to tell—
ran to meet him, whose wretched mind a black spirit
filled, tearing at it with the unclean power of frenzy.
He found it a welcome home to dwell among grim tombs;
no one could restrain his violent frenzy;
indeed, he would even burst strong bonds of iron
and tear heavy chains like woollen threads.
And now it was his sport to leap nimbly about with his fetters loosed
and to gash his savage breast with stones.
When he saw Christ making his way along the shore,
he rushed out with a shout and ran up from afar, worshipping him:
'Most certain offspring of the ever-reigning Lord,
we beg you not to drive us, racked with torments, far
from the borders of our accustomed region.
For our name is Legion, and many spirits under one
name are bound together by the single power of doing harm.
Do you see how the unclean swine root through these pastures?
At least let us glut our rage, driven back, on them;
we ask it by the exalted name of the high-throned Father.'
Christ commands them to leave the man's mind
and allows them to spend their fury in the herds of swine.
And now, the demon shaken out, the man's dazed heart
reveres the unhoped-for gift of his own healing.
And now the swine, hurled headlong from the edge of the cliffs
into the sea, hasten to lose their lives.
But the swineherds, terrified at such wonders from their lookouts,
scatter in flight and rush to the houses of the city
and kindle the report and drive the people to the shore.
But after the gathered crowd of onlookers
was forced to believe that the mad young man had come to his senses,
they begged in fear that he would leave that region.
Then Jesus, light of the world, makes his way back home.
Lo, as he returned, they laid before Christ's feet, lying on a bed,
a young man's numbed limbs, whose use
a grievous disease had undone.
Pitying him in his heart, Jesus addresses him:
'Let sure steadfastness be in your mind, young man,
for the past errors of your life will be forgiven you.'
This saying the scribes, in the hidden depths of a malicious mind,
found fault with, because he had uttered words fit to be spoken only by the power
of God. But Christ, seeing such hearts,
said: 'This word the sayings of the scribes call into question.
But how much easier it was to say it, they shall find proved
by the power of the word and the deed that follow alike,
and they shall see that it is granted to me to forgive sins.
Therefore, young man, with the use of your body made firm,
rise up in strength and carry your bed back home.'
He rose, fitted the bed to shoulders now strong,
and went off in vigor through the midst of the marvelling people.
Then fear and praises of the Lord fill the hearts of the people
as together they celebrate the joyful miracles.
Going on from there, he saw at the tax office
Matthew, sitting in the midst of the assembly; at once, then,
he bids him cleave to the disciples. Refusing nothing,
he obeys Christ's command and follows him gladly.
Then, setting out on the road, he urges Philip with like words
and added him as a companion to his friends.
When Philip had come to know Christ's powers and way,
as soon as he met the righteous Nathanael,
he said: 'Behold, it has been granted to our age that he should arise
of whom the voices of the ancients and the holy prophets sang.
Joseph, sprung from the line of David, fathered him;
blessed Nazareth is his homeland, and his name is Jesus.'
Nathanael replies: 'I wonder whether Nazareth has ever produced anything
that was worthy of such great powers.'
Then Philip said: 'You will see; stop doubting.'
When Jesus caught sight of him approaching from afar,
he said: 'Here comes a man whose heart, knowing no falsehood,
keeps its virtue pure, without malicious guile.'
He answered: 'Where, or at what time, did you come to know me?'
To him the Lord utters these words from his divine heart:
'When the shade of the spreading fig tree covered you,
even before Philip's words called you,
the Author of the Spirit saw you and chose you as a companion.'
At these words comes the voice of astonished Nathanael:
'Venerable offspring of God, renowned king of our nation,
you are salvation made manifest to the peoples and the teacher of life.'
To this Christ said: 'A slight display of power persuaded you to believe,
because I saw you resting beneath the shade of a tree;
but greater wonders still remain hereafter.
You shall all see the whole heaven split open
and God's swift ministers pierce the upper air
and then bring down a shining crown to the Son of Man.'
Meanwhile a festive wedding was being prepared in the bridal chambers
in the region of Cana, where the mother of glorious Jesus
was taking part in the banquet together with her son.
But meanwhile the wine was running out for the guests.
Then his mother entreats Christ with these words:
'Do you see that the drink of gladness has now run out?
Let gifts given by you, my son, grace these good tables.'
Christ, the glory of the earth, answered her:
'You are in haste, mother; the time does not yet require me
to grant such gifts for people's nourishment.'
Then his mother, gladdened, calls the servants of the tables
and bade them obey her son's commands.
There were six very beautiful vessels of hollowed stone,
whose bellies held three measures each.
These he bids the servants fill from the bosom of the spring.
The young men obey his orders and crown the stone vessels
with water, filling them to the lips; then foam along the edges
rolls the air mixed with the water up to the top.
Then he bids them hand it to the chief steward to taste.
When he had taken in the gift of that wondrous flavor,
not knowing that into the pleasant drink of wine
the water lately drawn from pure springs had turned,
he chides the unknowing bridegroom because, keeping back the fine wine,
he had first served the poorer wines around the tables.
By these signs, in the disciples who rightly believed,
he made their minds steadfast for ever with firm strength.
Then, when the Jews' solemn feast of the Passover was at hand,
he directed his way to Jerusalem and went up into the temple.
Here he found people setting out many goods for sale:
some were selling sheep, some the great bodies of bullocks,
some, gaping after coins, were busy counting them with skill.
Here Christ ties cords together into the lashes of a whip
and drives such people from the holy house,
and, overturning the tables, scatters the heaps of coins,
and rebukes them besides: 'Take these things far away, you profane,
so that here my Father, not sordid gain, may be worshipped.'
Then the Jewish people murmured, demanding a sign
in reliance on which he had raised his spirit to such deeds.
Then Christ wove things to come into obscure words like these:
'Destroy with polluted hands this venerable temple;
I will restore it when the sun's third light
begins to pour its ruddy rays upon the earth.'
They, debating among themselves in a hidden murmur,
said: 'This temple, built over barely forty-six years
by the toil of the ancient kingdom,
will you be able to renew in the space of three days?'
This saying worthy men in time, after the appointed days,
came to understand: that Christ had spoken of his own body
as the shrine of God. But seeing the signs,
many then took up faith and followed the Holy One.
Under cover of dark night one raised to lofty honor,
one of the foremost leaders of the Jewish people,
came and spoke to Christ in a lowered voice:
'There is no doubt, Holy One, that the bountiful will of God
has granted you to rise as a light upon human affairs;
nor would anyone perform wonders with such great signs
unless the power of God, accompanying him, bade them shine forth.'
To this Christ said: 'If you seek the heights of the righteous path,
no one will be able to ascend to the lofty kingdom
unless he enters once more into the beginnings of birth, given back to him,
and receives new life by a divine gift.'
But he, astounded at heart by such sayings,
said: 'This is beyond our mind to grasp.
Who could call back the beginnings of a life already begun?
Or should an old man creep back into his mother's womb
to come new into the light and live his life over again?'
He answered: 'If anyone, reborn from the clear spring
and from the Holy Breath, begins to stand with new limbs,
he will ascend free into the heavenly hall.
An earthly body is born of an earthly body;
in just the same way the Spirit begets a breath like itself.
This Spirit is God, whom all things in the world obey.
He flies wherever he wills and casts his voice through the air,
but you do not know where that voice begins
or toward what region his rushing blasts are bound.
So whoever returns to the first beginnings of a righteous life,
it is certain that he grows green again, like the Holy Breath.'
And the Jew replied: 'I can see none of these things.'
Then Christ said: 'Great teacher of Jerusalem,
do you too, pitiable man, take a mind snatched from the light of life
and plunge it headlong into murky darkness,
unable to grasp such things with your dulled sense?
Look, there is no faith, though I have spoken only of earthly things!
What if my speech should begin to ascend to heavenly powers
and to grasp the higher forms of things?
Which of you will be able to open his hard mind to me?
Hear, then, what the meaning of these new things is.
No one will be able to ascend to the starry heaven
except him alone who has come, sent from the hall of heaven,
the Son of Man, the same who dwells in heaven's seat.
As once in the desert regions the serpent
was lifted up in highest honor by the hands of Moses,
so the Son of Man must be lifted up on high,
so that whoever, in the deep recesses of his mind,
sets his faith on his name may, amid the whirlwind of the age,
trample death underfoot and, rising beyond the stars,
receive on high the inviolable gift of life.
For God loved the world with such great love
that his only offspring came down to earth
to join believers to the Lord in a bond of everlasting life.
Nor did God send this Son to search the earth with severe law
or to weigh it in harsh judgment,
but that the gentle gifts of life might come to the peoples.
For where sure faith has embraced salvation,
there will be no uncertain trial at law.
But where the gifts of healing have been shut far out,
their own condemnation already torments their minds;
for the only offspring of the Lord remained unknown to them.
The wretched proud fled the coming of the light
and preferred to embrace and hold fast to blind darkness.
So whoever has stained his mind with evil deeds
flees in fear into darkness, lest in the clear light
the sordid infection of his polluted mind be laid bare.
But whoever has kept to the footsteps of a godly life
hastens into the open and rejoices to shine in the light,
so that the glory of virtue may gleam in his bright deeds.'
Then Jesus the Savior heads back to Galilee.
But on his way he happened to come to Sychar in Samaria.
There was a field there, renowned for the name of Jacob,
and a well sunk deep into hidden depths, with a cold spring.
Here the Savior had sat down, panting in the scorching heat,
and the disciples, buying food within the city walls,
scattered here and there, had left their master alone.
Coming out from the walls, a Samaritan woman came
to draw water from the hollow depths of the well.
Christ said to her: 'Woman, give me a drink of water.'
The woman answered: 'It is a strange thing you ask of me,
that I, a Samaritan woman, should serve a drink to you, a Jew,
spurning the commands of the Samaritans of old.'
Then the Savior said: 'If you knew the gifts of the Lord,
and who it is that, thirsting, asks you for a drink from the well,
you would rather have asked, and he would give you living water.'
To this she said: 'The well curves its bosom deep down,
there is no pitcher, and you have no rope to let down;
from where, then, can you give me living water?
Surely you are not greater in power than our father?
For Jacob drank from this well with his children,
and often led his own flocks here to drink.'
Jesus, ruler of the world, answered her:
'No one will be fully satisfied by that water,
for he will thirst again; but the gifts of our water
will shut out the burning need to drink for all eternity.
Whoever receives the sweet cups of our spring,
from him the grace of a life-giving stream will flow more abundantly.
But if desire for our water has taken hold of you,
let your husband be called and come with you soon from the city.'
The woman says that she is not bound in marriage.
Then Jesus, who sees into minds, continues thus:
'Woman, you speak truthful words about a husband.
For you have already been joined in marriage to five men,
and now, besides, you take up the bonds of another's bed.'
Then the woman said: 'It is certain that you are a holy prophet.
But our fathers once left us a precept
to worship on the venerable summit of this mountain of ours,
while you say that prayer must be made in the land of Jerusalem.'
As she said this, Jesus at once replied:
'Behold, the time will come when from the peak of your mountain
and from all Jerusalem worship will be far removed.
But now sure salvation will rise from the land of the Jews,
and now the course of the coming time is pressing on,
when true worshippers, with error removed,
will pray to the holy Father, armed with righteous laws.
In them will be the Spirit and full faith, and the Father on high
seeks such hearts of worshippers on earth.'
She then said: 'We know that the Christ, a messenger to the world,
will open up the ages of life by his coming.'
And then Jesus, the bountiful pitier of the sinner,
declares that he is the Christ, come as a light to the world.
And now the disciples, returning, were amazed at their master,
that a woman was enjoying private conversation with him.
But the woman, hurrying, left her jar at the spring
and led the people out from the whole city.
For she relates that all the things she herself had done before
had been told her, one by one, in the prophet's words.
Then the crowds poured out and quickly sought Christ.
Meanwhile the disciples kept urging him to take some food.
He answered that he had fine food enough
to spare. But then among the wondering disciples
talk ran back and forth in secret whispers:
'Perhaps someone here has given our master a meal before us,
so that, being full, he rightly refuses our food.'
But he, perceiving the workings of their inner minds, said:
'This is my meal; this heart will be satisfied
if I carry out the commands of my great Father throughout the world.
You surely think that four months still remain
of fruitful summer before the start of the glad harvest.
Lift up your eyes, then, behold the whitening fields,
and all the countryside already calling for the ripe harvest.
Now whoever reaps will rejoice in the reward of his fine labor
and will then overflow with life-giving fruit,
and the sower, glad, will share the joys of the reapers.
I have now sent you to cut down a heavy harvest
that was not sown in the furrows by your labor.
Others' gifts of good fruit will enrich you.'
While he fills his companions' hearts with such words,
lo, the Samaritan people came asking
and entreat him to spend two days there.
And now deep faith had grounded many of the people;
no longer did they trust only the woman's words,
but power manifest before their eyes taught them
that Jesus, the Savior of the world, had now come.
And now he had returned to the region of Galilee,
where once he had changed spring water into wine.
Here a royal young man, whose son a disease with panting
fever was scorching at the very edge of life,
when he learned for certain that Christ had come back,
flies to him and, pouring out prayers for his child's fate,
begged him, pleading for the gift of swift healing,
before his son should be dragged off to bitter death.
To this Christ said: 'Unless power proves everything with signs,
there will be no faith; but go, and in your house
embrace your dear son, his life safe and sound.'
At these words a fair faith, soon to reap the fruit of healing,
steadies his mind in his rejoicing breast.
And now, as he set out, servants hurrying to meet him
brought the news that to the boy, out of the threshold of death,
sudden health had returned, into the realm of light.
When he learned that the time exactly matched
the words of Christ the healer, he gave over himself and his household,
embracing the venerable gift of faith.
It chanced that a day had brought together at one feast many
who, having contracted for the public taxes for profit,
openly seize plunder in another's name.
Jesus received these together with his disciples.
Lo, the Pharisees found fault with secret laughter
that a teacher of the law should join such banquets.
But he, looking into what their closed hearts held,
said: 'There is no need of physicians where strong limbs
are kept vigorous by unimpaired health in the pride of their strength.
But healing must rightly be given to the wretched sick.
Learn now at least what the prophet's words command:
"I seek not sacrifices so much as gentle hearts."
For I have not come to the righteous who walk the straight way,
but to call back the steps of the wicked from the path of sinners.'
But lo, from among those marvelling at Christ's gifts,
one of John's disciples asked
why they themselves kept the frequent fasts of the law
while the people under Christ kept no fasts.
Christ replies to this with calm countenance:
'Those who attend the bridegroom's wedding with joyful dances
do not keep sad fasts while he is present.
But the day will come when the bridegroom, by the whirlwind of the age,
will be snatched from the midst of his companions: then they
will give up their hearts to mournful tears and loathing of food.
How foolish it is to sew old rags onto new garments,
so that an ugly tear gapes open worse!
Or to pour hot new wine into worn-out wineskins,
which burst, so that all the living wine is lost!
Rather, it is right to store foaming new wine in new skins:
so strong vessels preserve the living wine.'
As he was speaking of such things, lo, his heart stricken with grief,
a chief of the priests falls prostrate, worshipping,
and for his dead daughter—a pitiable death—
he pleads with tears, and begged that the gifts of Christ
might bring sure healing even to the dead.
Without delay Jesus the Savior rises and sets out.
As he went on, a woman followed, keeping to his footsteps,
whom for twelve slipping years, with grievous sickness,
an unending flow of blood had been wasting away,
her strength consumed and her whole body worn out.
Believing, she was silently turning over in the secret
of her heart, and held with faith already sure,
that at once the wasting would leave her weary body
if she could touch the hem of Christ's garment.
When, through the crowd, with trembling hand she touched
the threads hanging from the hem of his robe, he at once,
seeing both the cause of the disease and her believing heart,
granted swift healing with these words:
'Receive the gift your steadfast faith has earned.'
And at once the blood was stanched and her veins grew strong.
When they came to where the girl's funeral was, and the great
wailing of the mourning people and the blare of trumpets
were performing the last rites of the final procession,
he said: 'Let these sad things leave your house.
For the girl lies sunk in peaceful sleep,
though the weeping crowd, not knowing, thinks her dead.'
As he said this, the crowd laughed and left him,
because he said that a girl snatched away by death was sleeping.
But Christ, conqueror of death and restorer of life,
deigning to take her cold right hand in his own,
soon bade her rise, to her father's wondering joy.
Then, as he went back, a cry at once met him
from two blind men together, stumbling as they walked.
Christ said to them: 'What do your hearts believe?
Will the light taken from you be restored by my power?'
They declare that they believe with a steadfast heart.
Then Christ said: 'Since you believe, behold the light,
and from now on tell no one our name.'
So he spoke; but at once, amid such great joy, the unquenchable
eagerness of those who now could see spread the report everywhere.
Next a young man is brought to him, whose power
of sounding speech had been taken away by a demon's attack.
But when the demon, driven out, fled from his breast,
at once the gift of a sound tongue returned.
He is hemmed in by the thronging tumult of a people
marvelling at such things; but seeing so many thousands of men,
he groans like the owner of an estate whose rich pastures
are grazed by countless sheep that lack a shepherd.
Then he speaks these words to his disciples:
'How rich the crops spread out across the countryside!
But the few reapers are overwhelmed by the heaps of grain.
It remains now to beg the lord of so great a harvest
to be willing to fill his fields with a host of laborers.'
Having said this, he gathers apart, chosen from all the people,
strong hearts into a company of twelve.
When he had chosen them, he fills them with these precepts:
'Avoid the road that the faithless nations
tread, and the footsteps of the deceitful Samaritans.
Go where the keeping of our ancestral flock is failing.
And as you go, take on a mind like mine,
so that holy faith may subdue for you the powers of the black demon
and apply loving care to sicknesses.
These powers will be given to you without payment,
and you likewise must bestow your gifts freely.
Let no possession of gold or silver master your mind,
nor let wicked desire for money overcome you.
Let the minister of bare virtue not wish to keep
two garments, nor a double covering for his feet.
When you enter the walls of a city, always seek out
those whose hospitality it is fitting for the righteous to accept;
and when you have entered, call down peace upon the house.
If the household is peaceable, that peace will remain;
but if it bristles with the unworthy ways of those who dwell there,
it will flee, and your peace will follow you as you leave.
Whoever savagely shuts you out from the threshold of his house,
or with hardened ears spurns the words of life,
shake off your footprints as you leave their homes,
lest any share in an unrighteous life cling to you.
A worse penalty than that of Sodom will await them
in torments, when the end comes to the whole world.
Go now like sheep, the prey of cruel wolves;
but be strong with the shrewd heart of serpents,
yet surpass the gentle doves in simplicity.
For often headlong injury will fall upon you,
and your bodies will be brought before the councils of men.
With whips and cruel chains and harsh tyrants
the gnashing violence of the age will press hard on you because of me.
When they hand you over, put aside all worry about words;
the grace of speech will be given you, flowing of its own accord;
the Spirit within you will speak fitting words on your behalf.
For a brother's wicked madness will betray his brother,
and children will give up their parents' bodies to death.
Hatred will always press upon you for the sake of our name,
but the glory of life attends faith that holds to the end.
Flee from the houses of a city that persecutes you;
seek out another home from there, and soon from there another.
For there must always be cities left for you
to furnish a people under the name of Israelites.
A disciple should never rise above the lofty heights
of his master, nor a servant try to surpass his lord.
It is enough for a disciple to equal his master's strength,
or for a servant to attain a worth like his lord's.
Let all fear stay far from your hearts at all times;
for all things are brought out, stripped from their hiding places.
Whatever you are told quietly in the darkness,
speak it in the brilliant light of the shining sun.
And whatever I say, whispering in your ears,
let it be scattered among the peoples from the high housetop.
Scorn the rage of those who will lay your bodies
low with the sword: they have no power
to send the living mind to death along with them.
Rather, let the heart's secret depths dread him
who has all power over body and soul together.
Sparrows will fetch a price of scarcely a small fraction
of a coin; yet one must not believe that a single one
runs into our snares without the Lord's command.
What wise man would doubt that, in the Lord's heart,
many thousands of winged creatures give way to one man?
Whoever confesses me before an earthly judge,
him I shall acknowledge in just the same way before my Father;
likewise, before my Father I shall deny the one who denies me.
I have not come now to send peace upon the earth,
but a sword, to cut a son away from his father's breast
and to cut a sweet daughter away from her mother's breast.
If anyone holds his father dearer than his love for me,
or puts his love for me behind his mother or his children,
he will suffer a terrible rejection from our dwelling.
Whoever despises his life for the sake of our name
will find it flourishing with the glad harvest of salvation.
Whoever receives you will rejoice that he has received me
with kindly service, and likewise that in receiving me he has received
the supreme Father for himself, in everlasting life."
When he had given such commands to the twelve disciples,
righteous John, from the shadows of his dark prison,
orders men chosen from among his followers
to carry these words to Christ and bring back the truth:
"Are you the rest for devout souls which the palace of heaven
promised to the earth, now shining forth in our time?
Or must we still hope for another salvation after this?"
Christ sends back his reply in these words:
"The darkness of the blind is changed into the light of day,
and the limbs of the weak thrive with strength made firm;
pallid leprosy is shaken off the scaly body,
and the sound of the voice in the air pierces deaf ears.
To life that was lost, after the funeral rites of death,
the soul's power, already set free, is restored, returning to the body;
and to its own poor, not disdaining them, there is opened
the shining glory of our resplendent coming.
Blessed will he be whom error has not deceived."
The disciples carry this message back to their master.
Upon this Christ sets forth these words to the people:
"Why did you lately wish to go out into the wilderness to see
a reed stalk swaying in the shaking wind?
Why, again, to see a man dressed in soft clothing?
Those in soft clothing are kept in the houses of kings.
He alone was promised long ago to surpass the powers of the prophets
by the verdict of the ancient Scripture.
For the reading of the venerable word speaks of him:
Behold, I send my servant to prepare the roads
before your face. No woman has ever borne anyone
who was greater in strength than our John.
Yet one less than he will be loftier in the hall of heaven.
From his rising onward, the kingdom of heaven feels force,
and fierce violence seizes the kingdom of heaven.
The whole Law reached its fulfillment in the time of the Baptist,
and there too the end of the prophets is concluded.
If you wish to know the inner secrets of this fleeting age,
the body of John was taken as a dwelling by blessed
Elijah, whom once, sent down in a flashing whirlwind,
the likeness of a four-horse chariot with fiery hooves carried away.
Let him hear these things who opens his ears to life-giving words.
Now I praise you, Father, whom the glory serves
of the shining heaven and of the fruitful lands,
because you have now hidden these things from the proud and wise
and willed that the little hearts of infants should grasp them.
All things of my reigning Father have now been handed over to me,
and no one will be able to know the Son of the Lord
except the Father alone; and the Son will see the Father with his mind,
or he to whom the same Son reveals such things.
Let all come here whom the load of a vast burden
weighs down; for them my power, by the Father's gift, can
restore their former strength with glad rest.
Take up the yoke bravely; my burden is light for the just,
for it bestows sweet salvation on the humble heart."
When he had said this, he passed through fields of heavy-laden harvest,
and the band of disciples following him
were plucking the full grain of the ears as they went along.
That day demanded rest under the ancient law,
for the Sabbath renewed its leisure by ancient commands.
Look: the Pharisees openly rebuke Christ
because, in reaping, his disciples were trampling on the commands of the holy law.
But then Jesus, the fulfiller of the laws,
begins thus, unrolling the records of the ancient Scripture:
"Surely you have read that David the singer, in the temple,
once took the consecrated loaves together with his people
and satisfied his own hunger and his companions'; yet those
loaves were unlawful for anyone to touch,
since by law only the priest could take them.
By the just governance of the same law it is written:
Priests may profane the Sabbath in the temple without guilt.
Nor is what stands here amid your gathered crowd any less
than the power of the temple. If your hearts could grasp
that God prefers not sacrifices but gentle hearts,
your faction would not so often have condemned holy men
who were free of guilt. But now, of my own will,
I shall hold every Sabbath as its lord, by right of the law."
Then, after these words, he enters their synagogue;
soon he sees there, at the threshold, a young man
from whose shoulder hung the useless weight of a withered
hand. But then, testing him with deceitful words,
they ask whether it is lawful to bring healing to the sick on the Sabbath,
so that punishment for a trampled law might await him.
Christ answers: "If by chance your little flocks
fall into a pit, you will surely set aside the law's rest
and lift the paltry beast out of the steep depths.
How much more, then, should the healing of men
kindle our minds and lift them to good deeds!
Come then, young man, stretch out your restored right hand."
At the word he stretched out both hands, healed.
Then, for these signs, which a marveling people's reverence
could scarcely exalt with worthy honor,
they cry out in savage councils that he must be trapped.
Christ, seeing such schemes of the leaders,
withdraws; to the various illnesses of men he applies
the healing granted to the peoples by his Father's power.
Soon a man was brought to him whom the horrid power of a demon
willed to live maimed in tongue and sight, for punishment,
and to be food for his own torments.
When the blind faction of the Pharisees' race
learned he was healed and strong in sight and voice,
they claim that by the help of a demon, who as prince of demons
alone held the forces of wickedness under his command,
he had done these things. But Christ lays such hearts
bare, refuting them with truthful words:
"If a kingdom, torn apart, splits into two parts
and the divided rift fights against itself,
everything will quickly collapse, its very marrow burst apart.
And if a horrid demon is driven out by a black demon,
he is split and fights against himself with opposing power.
Who can carry off plunder from men's houses
unless the attacker first binds the arms of the guards
with knots, so that seizing the spoil may come easily?
Every soldier who stands apart, cut off from my arms,
will stand as an enemy on the opposing front of battle.
Whoever wanders off free from gathering my flocks
scatters my grazing herd through trackless places.
But whatever error men may commit in anything,
it can be forgiven; only let the Spirit never
be torn by words poured out from a mad mind.
Even if anyone in fury heaps insults on the Son of Man,
these sins too can be forgiven.
But whoever violates the Holy Spirit alone with the profane
rage of words will be scorched by fire in irrevocable
punishments, now and forever.
When will the savage brood of the venomous serpent
be able to grow mild with the sweet fruit of words?
For good and sweet things are brought out of just treasuries,
and evil poisons come forth from a deadly mouth.
By the merit of words punishment will come before the judge;
by the merit of words life will be given before the judge.
Whatever the Father does, the Son will follow in all things,
for the same Father shows the Son all things to be seen,
and hereafter he will grant still greater wonders.
For just as the Father will restore dead bodies
to the bright light of life, so the Son will lead all
the bodies he wills to rise up to the light;
nor will the Father, as judge, examine anything of yours,
but he has given the Son the right of inquiry throughout the world,
so that equal glory may remain to Son and Father.
For if the Son is refused your honor,
with equal wickedness you will despise the Father.
But whoever has faith fixed in him by the grace of our word,
to him the gifts of the Father who sent me will soon be revealed,
and his present steadfastness will give him eternal life.
For him there is no judgment; he passes far away from dark
