death and, full of vigor, makes for the threshold of light.
The time will come when dead bodies will hear
our voice, and with the voice will receive life.
For just as the Father possesses life in himself,
so he has granted life to the Son and bidden him pronounce judgment,
since he has come to the earth in the body of a man.
Do not be amazed that all bodies
rise from their own tombs at the hearing of the voice,
that the souls of the just are joined to bodies brought back to life,
and the wretched wicked rise to grievous judgment.
Nor does my own power alone grant me judgment,
since all things are commanded by the Father's will,
who bade me seek out justice on the earth.
For if I stand up as a witness on my own behalf,
I shall speak falsely; and since there is likewise another witness
on our behalf, it is always right for me to set such testimony aside.
For by the true signs of my works, brighter than all
light, the present testimony shines out in our deeds.
In granting these things, the Father stands by me as witness,
who sent me to the earth to establish his commands.
His voice you have never been able to grasp,
nor has he allowed you to see his own form.
Nor can his word settle within your
hearts, since you have no substance of belief.
Search the readings of the ancient Scriptures,
which you think bring everlasting life to all.
Those very readings bear witness to our gift.
Yet you do not dare to stand closer to us,
lest the grace of true life should befall you.
It is not the glory of earthly praise that I seek.
For that I have come in the name of the supreme Father
is rejected by you; but another will come, a tarnished one,
whom your nation will follow, though he leans on his own humanity alone.
Among you the glory of mutual fame is sought after,
and you shun seeking the praise that comes from the One alone.
Nor would I accuse you before the Father; but there
your accuser will be the one your hope now celebrates,
Moses, whom you have honored with no faith at all.
For if your error believed his writings,
it would believe us too, of whom the writings of Moses often speak."
Then these words of the scribes follow in reply:
"Undoubting faith will accompany these words
if power confirms the miracles with sure signs."
He then: "A generation polluted with evils seeks
signs for itself; but the signs will stand in things to come.
For as long as the prophet spent in the hollow belly
of the whale, so long, in the deep recesses of the earth,
will the Son of Man remain sunk.
The time will come when there will rise, restored to life,
a race of men who gave themselves up to weeping for their deeds.
They will condemn this nation for its well-deserved crime,
because, warned by the voice of the prophet rising
from the sea floor, they fell prostrate in tears and turned the Lord back.
Here, too, things greater than Jonah's warnings are commanded,
and the impious nation, with savage spirits, scorns the light.
And the queen of the South will rise into the realms of life.
By her example the savage people will be condemned,
because she came from the farthest bounds of Libya
to hear pious Solomon, devoted to the precepts he taught;
now there is a power greater than Solomon,
and yet the hearts of the dull people are blinded.
If ever a demon, driven out, flees from the breast,
troubled by the holy breath in a body made clean,
he wanders with venomous steps through regions
where no water of a spring-fed stream runs out,
and, burning, he finds no rest for himself in a quiet abode.
Then, thirsting, he seeks again the familiar dwelling of the mind.
And if by chance he sees a heart open to his poisons
and a threshold smiling with frivolous adornment,
he gathers and joins to himself seven furies like himself,
a force hostile to man, and like a serpent he enters his inmost parts.
So when this race has fallen away from the true mind,
bound in chains, it will lament in everlasting punishments."
And while he was repeating these life-giving words to the people,
his mother stood with his brothers before the doors
and asked to speak with him face to face outside.
Then he sends back these words in reply to his mother's message:
"Here with me sits my mother, here with me sit my brothers
in body. For whoever fulfills my Father's will
joins his own body to my blood
and is counted under the name of my mother and my kin."
Jesus, the light of the world, goes forth from the temple
and sat down at the edge where sea and land meet,
and countless crowds of people streamed there.
But he, climbing into a tall ship that lay nearest,
sets forth these things to the people filling the shore:
"Behold, a sower entrusts seeds to his own field;
they fall on differing ground and receive the lot of their places
according to its quality. For wherever, on trodden roads,
the earth is packed by feet into a solid path,
the seeds lie as bare prey for the birds of the air.
But where rocks are veiled with a very thin layer of dust,
the grain does indeed put forth the green rising of a shoot;
but because the clods have no store of moisture beneath,
the threads of the roots dry up as the heat gets in,
and soon all the tips of the blades sink down to death.
Other seeds meet with rough fields;
here, from brambles and wild thorns, there springs up more swiftly
a woody growth, which chokes and kills the crop.
But the seeds that are given to rich soil
bear a beautiful crop, whose glad increase
abundance multiplies with a hundredfold yield.
Let him hear this who has the ears of his mind open."
The disciples, marveling at such words, ask
why he was shutting up everything from the people in tangled words;
but he, having drawn the believers apart from the crowd, says:
"To you, who with steadfast hearts have made your minds strong
to grasp the inner secrets of God,
it is granted to stand deep within the sanctuaries of the kingdom;
for them, as they deserve, the eyes of the mind are shut.
If anyone who is worthy has, he will receive more, in overflowing measure;
but those who wander without the heavenly gift
will lose even whatever they keep as their own.
That is why the grace of our speech only grazes that people,
wrapped in obscure riddles,
so that Isaiah's saying about this deserving people may come true again:
Behold, the minds of the people are veiled to all things by thick
barriers, so that they do not touch the gifts of life with understanding.
They stand by with closed ears and heavy eyes,
lest the guilty people be turned to good and healed.
How blessed now are your ears and eyes!
For many righteous men of old and holy prophets
prayed to see the gifts that shine clear before you.
Take to heart, then, what the meaning of the seed is:
Whoever lets my word in only at the surface of his ears
and does not take in the precepts with steady strength of understanding,
from his heart the devil snatches it all away.
He is like the hard field, which lays out the seeds of grain
as plunder for swift birds, yielding no harvest.
There are others who receive our words with a glad heart,
but the grace of the harvest they received is short-lived for them.
For if harsh constraint presses on their mind and hems it in,
at once in fear they betray to death what was entrusted to them.
For them the rocky field grows green with a like shallowness.
But the thorny field answers to those weighed down by a mass
of cares, whom the burdens of riches oppress.
So the seeds of our word are pressed and weighed down,
and no fruit follows, killed by the bristling thorns.
In just the same way, the rich fields stand with equal strength
for those who receive the precepts of shining salvation,
which penetrate the mind as understanding holds them fast,
and bear a hundredfold harvest by the strength of virtue."
Then he adds these further words for the disciples and the people:
"The lofty kingdom of the Thunderer is like a farmer.
He sows, entrusting good seeds to his own field,
but afterwards, stealing in and lying in wait for men's sleep,
a savage enemy comes and scatters bitter darnel.
But see, when the bristling ear on its stalk
has come forth to fruit, the harvest overflows, stained with darnel.
Then the servants, marveling, speak thus to their master:
Did you not sow good seed across the face of the earth?
Where, then, does the foul darnel come from that burdens your fields?
But now, if you command, we will clear the whole harvest,
and the gleaming wheat will remain once the filth is picked out.
Then the master answers with gentle words:
This is your trickery, enemy; but let us allow the grain
to grow with the darnel. For at the full time of harvest
I will order the darnel to be separated, bound in sheaves,
and burned in the fire; but the reaper will then fill our barns
with the cleansed grain from our seed.
In the same way, if you open the ears of your heart,
the kingdom of heaven is like a tiny grain of mustard
which a farmer plants and sets in his own little field.
It is thought to be the smallest of all the seeds
of green plants; but once it has taken on the full growth
of its proper greenness, it rises with lofty crown above all
the crops of the fields, so that the feathered throng
can play among its branches and dwell in its green shade.
The heavenly gift is like wholesome leaven,
which a woman hides in a great mass of flour.
Then that flour, mixed with the slight warmth of the leaven
worked through it, grows together into the body of a single mass."
Such things, hidden in tangled words, he then set forth
to the people, so that the words of the ancient prophet
might accord, in the order of the ages, with the events ordained:
I will deign to open my mouth; things hidden since the world's foundation
the image of varied speech will unfold as it pours them forth.
Then, late in the day, he returns home and left the crowds behind.
BOOK THREE.
The fiery-haired sun had poured its rosy radiance over the earth.
The disciples ask what the riddle of the darnel
and the wheat might mean, and glorious Jesus explains it to them:
'He who entrusts the finest seeds of grain to the soil
is the Son of Man. By the field, understand the world,
and by the pure seed, righteous men.
But the barren darnel, sown by the craft of the hidden demon,
is wicked men; the enemy, that dreadful power, is the demon;
the final end of the world stands for the time of harvest.
The reapers who will come through the fields are the Father's ministers,
whom the Son of Man will command to gather out of the body of his own kingdom
the snares of error and every stain,
and, once gathered, to burn them all together in devouring flames.
For these there will be gnashing of teeth forever and unending weeping,
but to the righteous, set apart, the golden light of life will come,
as the rays of the sun shimmer in the dwellings of heaven.'
This he taught, and the Saviour returns to his home town.
There, setting out for the people — wonderful to tell —
the laws of righteousness and the wholesome commands of life,
he taught, and at the same time brought in the mighty works of his Father.
Then the common folk of his own people, stirred by bitter envy,
turning over the miracles of the gift before their eyes
and reckoning up his family line from a lineage they knew,
mutter these words among themselves:
'Is this not the son of the carpenter whose name is Joseph?
Is not Mary his mother, and are his brothers not a family we know?
Where, then, does this teacher of the law come from, this minister
of such great power, before whom the plague of evils yields, defeated?'
So spoke the people of Nazareth, and Jesus answers them thus:
'Miracles are always scorned in one's own country,
and prophets remain without honour in their native place.'
Indignant at this, Christ held back his gifts.
Meanwhile word flew to the proud king
that a divine power was subduing every evil.
But Herod thinks that John, released from the law of death,
possessed such great gifts of power.
For once the demon, seeing with envious heart
that righteous John was washing away the stain of error
in pure waters, was inflamed by the losses dealt to evil,
and that most savage plague then made for King Herod.
Easily entering the dwelling of an unjust heart,
it drives him to heap impious crimes upon savage deeds.
Herod had burned, kindled by an unlawful love,
for his brother's marriage-bed, which John, learned in the law of chastity,
forbade. But savagery that knows nothing of right
trampled the laws underfoot and enjoys the unspeakable
marriage, and the very man who forbade the wickedness
he plunged into the darkness of prison and weighed down with chains.
For at first, held in check by fear, that savagery,
though thirsting for the righteous man's blood, held back, because the great reverence
of the people upheld John as a prophet.
But it happened that on his birthday, when the tyrant Herod
was laying out a joyful banquet at lofty tables —
for pride delights in the company of luxury —
in the midst of the young men the queen's daughter, a maiden,
quickening the alternating sway of her sides in sinuous movement,
joins in dances set to a measured song.
But the king above all, marvelling at the maiden's art,
stood spellbound; then on oath he promises that every reward lies open to her,
whatever the girl might ask.
But she, carrying out the impious crimes of her dreadful mother,
presses for John's head to be torn from his neck
and brought in on a platter, demanding the gift on the spot.
Herod, sorrowful, yet under the weight of the nobles present
and mindful of the bond of his oath, reluctantly commands
that the innocent man's head be brought in and handed to the girl.
She — the outrage! — wicked girl, carries it to her mother for her delight.
But his disciples, weeping, bury in the earth the mangled, nameless trunk
of his body, and follow Christ.
When he learned of the righteous man's pitiable death,
he leaves the land polluted with innocent blood
and hides in the leafy shade of a secluded valley.
But the people follow the gifts of his boundless power.
When he sees that crowds of believers had gathered
in the remote valley, he drove away the wasting of disease
and in his pity brought many bodies to healing.
And now, in the last light of the setting sun,
the disciples urge Christ to send the crowds away,
so that each might provide for himself, looking for food in the villages.
He orders a meal to be set out for all of them right there.
The disciples point out that there is no more food
than two fish and five pieces of bread.
'This,' he said, 'is enough.' Then at once he ordered the people to recline
and settle their limbs on couches of grass.
Then, looking up to heaven and praying to his Father,
he himself divides the two fish and the five loaves in turn
and loaded the tables with rich fare.
And now the people lie there satisfied — wonderful to tell —
and then the servers gathered the leftovers from the tables
and fill the hollows of twelve baskets with fragments.
The number of those who ate was five thousand men,
and besides them there was a crowd of mothers and children.
Then he orders the disciples to board a boat
and cross the sea, while he sent them all away,
each man to his home. Then he sought the heights of a mountain
and there, alone, worshipped the name of his Father.
And now all things lay still in the sleeping night,
while the boat was ploughing the waves in the middle of the sea,
tossed by the opposing blast of a rising wind.
But when, in the fourth watch, the morning star
was pressing on the course of night, lifting its swift rising,
on the liquid waves, with dry footsteps,
he was making his way, borne up — wonderful to see!
And now he was drawing near the boat, but the sailors, not knowing him,
were astounded, their hearts quivering with trembling fear,
and with confused minds they cried out together.
Then Christ speaks to the frightened men: 'Let all fear be gone,
and let quickening steadfastness rule the minds of believers.
See, it is I; recognize the teacher of your light.'
Peter confidently answered him thus:
'If it is truly your power that deigns to visit us,
let me likewise, at your command, upon the sea
plant my steps in the liquid waves.'
The Lord assented; Peter at once dares to leave the boat
and, leaning his weight upon it, plants his footsteps on the sea.
But when the marvel of such great things
terrifies his mind, and he sees the wind's threats growing stronger,
little by little, melted by doubting fear, the waters give way
which had borne up the strong force of his faith.
And now Simon, sunk to his waist, cries out:
'Snatch me from the dreadful waves, Christ, for I am perishing!'
At once a right hand is stretched out to meet Peter,
and his wavering faith is rebuked with bitter words,
and when he had boarded the boat the contrary winds abate.
And all whom chance had made companions on the boat
marvelled at the Son of God present among them and entreated him.
At last the boat, ploughing the seething waters, had crossed,
and the heavy anchor had gripped the longed-for harbour.
The people come running together along the shore,
carrying the sick, and long to touch the threads at the very edge
of his garment — and, wonderful to say, by this gift all
who believe carry home full health throughout their limbs.
Behold, the Pharisees and scribes, crafty on every side,
trying to trap Christ, bring out deceitful words:
'Why does your teaching allow your disciples to stray
from the precepts of the elders? For they have neglected
to wash their hands, and they take their food along with the dirt.'
To this he answers: 'It is more fitting to ask this:
why do you all transgress and betray the precepts of God?
For God by fixed law threatens death
if anyone's father is wounded by a bitter word,
or a mother assailed by the harsh speech of her son.
You make these void by teaching perverse things.
How plainly the prophet's words about you hold true:
"This people exalts me with honour on the surface of their lips,
but the secret places of their heart wander far off elsewhere."
Hear, then, all of you, and turn the ears of your heart to this:
whatever is put into a man will not spatter him
with shameful filth, nor settle in his life or mind.
But the things that burst out from the inner chambers of men's mouths,
once uttered, wretchedly stain the inner mind.'
The disciples tell Christ that the words he had spoken
had stirred the scribes' hearts to hidden mockery.
Then he said: 'Whatever seeds of plants our Father
has not himself sown in the expanse of his field,
he will tear up utterly by the roots and cast far away.
If a blind man happens to wander with a blind man for his guide,
both will fall together, plunged into the pit.'
Then Peter asks to have explained to him what the riddle meant
that he had just now put to the Pharisees and scribes.
Then the sower of eternal life answered thus:
'Do you too shut out all my commands with hard hearts,
and does the doubt in your minds not let in the light?
For whatever enters men's mouths from outside
passes into the belly and runs its course unknown to the mind.
But what men's mouths bring forth, conceived within the breast,
can defile the mind with the spattering of stain
and pollute a man with unclean guilt.
From the secret places of the heart come counsels harmful to life,
and murders, and the unspeakable theft of marriage beds,
and frauds, and men's deceit when they stand as witnesses,
and the madness of a reckless voice that beats against heaven.
These are what stain a man, what fill him with filth.
But to take earthly food with unwashed hands, as the body wishes,
never defiles anyone.'
When he had said this, he made for the beautiful countryside of Syria,
for Sidon and Tyre; there a woman with loosened
hair, pleading the cause of her daughter lying sick,
throws herself on the ground and anxiously never ceases to beg the silent Christ
to restore the mind tormented by a savage demon
and let the wretched girl at last come to her senses.
Then, even to the entreaties of the disciples following him,
he answered that he would rather gather his Father's own sheep,
whom vain error had scattered far and wide.
Then, as she pressed him more and more, Jesus says this:
'No one will ever take bread from his own children
and throw it to the dogs.' Then the woman says this:
'Yet at least the dogs have their share of crumbs
that fall from the table, and the masters' dinner is none the poorer.'
Then the Lord speaks: 'May the worthy rewards of salvation come to you,
which the strength of so great a faith has earned.'
Such were the heavenly words the Saviour spoke,
and his fruitful power, driving out the demon, embraced the girl's mind
and filled it with the gifts of salvation.
From there the Saviour returns to the region of Galilee
and sat down far off on the summit of a very high mountain.
Without delay the people gather, and some brought with them
those deprived of their eyes and a crowd with crippled legs,
others who were mute, and diseases of a thousand names.
Yet he took away their bitter afflictions from them all,
and bestows strong vigour on them as a gift to be revered.
Then the people throng together at such great miracles
and offer praise and thanks to the eternal Father.
Gathering the disciples on the mountaintop, Christ
speaks to them privately: 'Great is my pity for the people,
for already the third light of the sun is returning to the earth
since they took any food for themselves;
I would not want to send so great a crowd away fasting,
lest weariness overcome them as they travel the long roads.'
The disciples show Christ that they have seven loaves
and a few small fish as food at hand.
Then he ordered the people to recline on the surface of the ground,
and broke all there was with his own hands,
and had it given to all the people, table by table.
The disciples set out the meal and the people are filled
with food to their fill; soon they gather the fragments of bread
and bring back seven hampers heaped high.
There had been four thousand of the people in all,
and no one counted the mothers and children.
From there he crosses by boat to the region of Magadan.
Behold, the Pharisees and crafty Sadducees
press him, testing him, demanding signs from heaven.
But Christ, seeing their deceitful hearts, says:
'Whenever dewy night closes the vault of heaven,
if the evening comes on red from the starry sky,
you say, "Fair weather will come with tomorrow's light."
And at sunrise, when gloomy clouds
are mingled with red in a murky light,
you say that the crashing rage of the winds and the fury of storms
are coming upon farmers and sailors.
Deceivers, you know how to read the face of the sky,
yet do you not know how to search out the times of the ages
by their signs? But a sign will be given you,
the one that once came from the immense depths of the sea,
when the sea-beast held the prophet in the prison of its belly.'
So he spoke and, quickly loosing the boat's moorings,
hastens across the water to reach in swift course
the lands of Philip, and says this to his companions:
'Take care to avoid the harmful grain
and the fierce leaven: keep it away from your tables.
The Pharisees and crafty Sadducees
mix it into food and deceive under the name of bread.
Why does hesitation churn in your silent minds?
Ah, how small a faith grows faint with dull understanding!
You say, turning aside, that you had no time to take
loaves on board, and that this is why I bid you beware the snares
of grain. I thought you remembered and knew
that five loaves filled five thousand of the people for me
with food, and that so many baskets of leftover fragments
were collected into heaps of food,
and again that seven loaves easily filled
four thousand diners, and you saw hampers brought back
once more, full of leftovers.
But I warn you always to beware of their leaven.'
At last the disciples, following his life-giving words,
understand that he meant teaching by the name of leaven.
Then, when he had come across the surface of the liquid deep
to the famous countryside that bears the name of Philip,
he gathers a council of the disciples who followed him
and asks who the people's talk supposed him to be.
They answer that the people say many things:
they had often heard, and many affirm, that he was
righteous John, who washed the people in the river.
Some report words of winged rumour they had heard,
that Elijah had come again, whom once, in a swift chariot,
in a heavenly whirlwind shaped like a four-horse team,
the fervent force of rushing flame set among the stars.
Others said that Jeremiah the prophet had appeared.
Then Christ, smiling on them all with a kindly heart,
asks what the disciples' own opinion is.
But steadfast Peter said: 'You are the Son of the Holy One,
the Christ, who fill the earth with magnificent light.'
Then the Lord answered strong Peter thus:
'Peter, you will be blessed, for surely human blood
or the body, a portion of earth, could never
reveal such things. Only the gifts of the Father
can grant so strong a force of faith.
You uphold the name of Peter with fitting strength.
On this mass, on the strength of this rock, I will set
a house to stand forever with everlasting walls.
Against the gates of hell this house will have an unconquerable
bulwark, fortified with unending strength;
and it is my purpose to entrust to you the keys of the heavenly kingdom;
whatever you leave bound on earth by your judgment
will remain bound in heaven as well;
and again, whatever your sentence has loosed on earth
will be no less loosed in the dwelling of heaven.
But you, my disciples, refrain from telling everyone that I am the Christ,
so that only the worthy may know such things.
Already the day is coming, pressing upon me in hasty course,
when within the walls of Jerusalem a rage, rushing headlong in fury,
will glut the leading priests with my blood.
But when the third sun brings back its light-streaming dawn,
my life will rise again, crowned with the rays of salvation,
and will bestow its gifts on all the earth.'
Then Peter, struck to the heart with great grief, said:
'Christ, far be such grim portents from your holy
limbs! It is not right to believe so terrible a thing,
nor could so harsh a fate befall you.'
To this Christ said: 'Away from here, flee far away, devil!
Divine wisdom does not touch your mind,
but you think earthly thoughts and tremble with soft fear.
But if any of you will follow in my footsteps,
let him deny himself, renouncing body and soul,
and gladly add his own cross to my company;
glory will redeem for him the life he has lost,
for the possession of light, if kept on earth, perishes.
What will the mortal gains of this world profit
if they bring the loss of light and everlasting life?
Or what worthy exchange can be offered for the soul?
The Son of Man will come here in his Father's name,
and heavenly ministers will throng around him with a roaring escort,
and he will repay men what is due for their lives.
I tell you the truth: I will find some here still on the threshold of light
when I take possession, shining, of the kingdom of heaven.'
When he had said this, he let twice three days'
lights pass over the earth as the heavens turned,
and then he bids Peter and the two sons of Zebedee
climb a steep mountain with him by trackless ways.
When they had come to the summit of the secluded mountain,
at once Christ's face is transformed with flashing brightness,
and his garment shines with the whiteness of snow.
His companions look and see him standing in the midst
beside holy Elijah and Moses. Then Peter said:
'Consider whether it is better for us to go far away,
or to stay here and behold the spectacle of so great a thing;
yet, if you bid me, I will make three tents here for you,
separate ones, furnished with leafy boughs,
each a shelter to receive you at nightfall.'
While he was speaking, a brilliant cloud from heaven,
spread around their eyes, clothed the mountain in light,
and a voice rang out clearly from the midst of the light:
'This is my only Son, my highest delight;
take hold of his righteousness with a righteous heart.'
The disciples pressed their trembling bodies to the ground,
and did not dare to lift their faces from where they had fallen prone
until Christ's right hand, with holy touch,
soothed them and he strengthened their hearts with gentle words:
'Rise, be brave, cast off your fear and trample it underfoot,
and let no one be told in words of this vision,
until the glorious Son of Man returns here,
bringing back into the light trophies from the dwelling of death.'
They rise and see him alone, and ask him
why the faction of scribes insists, from the writings of the ancients,
that Elijah must first return from his dwelling in heaven
to earth, and only then the light of Christ arise.
To this Christ said: 'Elijah, at God's bidding, will come at an appointed time,
and soon restore to the world all that is due.
But, if anyone will believe it, he has already come before, born again,
and, as though he were unknown, the blind rage of fury
plunged him into death; and soon another, more savage slaughter,
see, threatens the Son of Man with cruel tearing.'
So he spoke, and leaves the mountain and returns to the people.
But behold, on bended knees and dissolved in tears,
an aged man, revering Christ with prayers, worships him:
'Son of David, light and salvation of mankind,
I beg you, drive this horrible sickness out of my son's body
and give an old man back the comforts of life.
For the course of the moon, by a demon's craft, torments my son
and hurls him down into the flowing waters,
or throws the poor boy into the middle of the fire and rolls him there.
For your disciples, following your commands, often
tried hard, but gave me no gift that lasted.'
Then Christ, moved to the heart with great grief, said:
'O faithless generation, a race forever savage,
how long am I still to bear being on earth with you?'
So he spoke, and orders the father to bring the boy
before his face. Then, with great weight of voice,
he pressed upon the demon, cleansed the boy's heart,
and put to flight the dreadful demon's poisons that had convulsed his mind.
The disciples ask why the cure of the same boy,
so often attempted, had not succeeded for them.
The Lord answered: 'Because in your breasts
the faltering step of unstable faith slips on slippery ground.
For if you had a sure share of belief,
even as much as the smallest mustard seed,
you could tear this mountain from here with a word
and roll its whole mass over to another place.
For this kind of sickness is driven off by unceasing prayers, by faith,
and by the many fasts of a strong heart.'
From there he went on foot to the region of Capernaum.
Those in charge of the tax came to Peter,
demanding that the customary payment be made on Christ's behalf.
But Christ turned to Peter and said this:
'Tell me, from whom have kings ordered tribute to be paid to them:
from foreigners' sons, or from their own?'
Peter answered: 'It is certain that strangers pay.'
'You see,' said Christ, 'that the king's son does not pay;
but so that I may give no offence, take up my command:
see that rock of the wave-sounding sea which juts out into the deep;
climb to its top, Simon, and cast a hook,
tied to a line of horsehair, headlong into the depths.
And whatever fish first catches on the curved point,
cut open the inner parts of its belly;
pay the double tax with what you find there.'
Afterwards the disciples ask who is greatest in the high
kingdom of heaven, and for what merits.
Then Christ orders a child to stand in the middle of the gathering,
and the teacher speaks out in calm words:
'Whoever desires to ascend to the lofty seat of heaven,
let him shape himself to be like this child in his ways.
It is certain that the snares of error will multiply in the world,
but woe to him through whom error comes.
Whoever leads astray any one of these little ones,
if he is wise, should tie a millstone around his neck
and hurl himself headlong into the waves of the sea.
And let no one in his pride despise these little ones.
Their guardians in the heavenly seat look upon
the face of the high-throned Father above the stars.
If a shepherd, whose hundred bleating sheep
graze the pastures entrusted to him, finds that one has by chance
strayed off unawares, he leaves them all and goes searching,
tracing the footprints of that one through all the woods,
to see if with great labour he can find it;
then greater joy arises over the lamb that is found
than over the whole flock because none had strayed.
So the Father does not allow any of these little ones
to be lost, and rejoices that they increase in his kingdom.
'If you see your own brother stained by a fault,
go at once and rebuke him with words, alone and in private.
If he patiently accepts and approves the guidance of your words,
you will have won, as a brother, the mind of your erring brother.
But if he scorns your words when you are alone and walks away,
then let other admonishers join you in repeating the holy commands.
But if he shakes off the reins of two teachers,
then let his offences be brought before the full assembly,
so that, overcome at least by the weight of the people, he may be healed.
But if in his savagery he scorns the voices of many as well,
let him be to you as one punished with the name of a foreign nation.
For my presence will always come into the assembly,
and I must stand in the midst of two,
or of three, if they gather in my name.'
Then Peter asks how many times he should forgive a brother's wrongs,
whether it might be right to forgive as many as seven lapses.
Christ continues: 'Not only seven offences,
but tenfold beyond that let a brother's wounds be forgiven.'
'For the kingdom of heaven is like the lord of a very wealthy household
who ordered his accounts to be set before him,
and commanded that a servant who owed many talents
be seized, with his wife and children
and all his goods, and put up for sale.
Then the servant prostrated himself and worshipped his lord,
and promised that, if only he were given some time,
he would pay his lord the whole sum of money.
Pity for the weeping servant moved the lord,
and beyond what he deserved he forgave the servant all his debts.
But as he went out, finding a fellow servant on the very threshold,
he seizes him; then, being the stronger, he demands his debts
be paid, ruthlessly refused all room for pleading,
and kept him sunk in the darkness of prison and punishment.
When the lord began to learn of this from the servants' reports,
he had the servant brought before him and heaped on him most just
words in his grief, and, stirring up his anger, with stern orders
thrust the cruel man into torments, recalling all
his debts, until in chains he should pay the penalty he deserved.
So will the Father who dwells on the heights of heaven do to you,
if with savage hearts you mercilessly choose to punish harshly
the sins of brothers who beg your forgiveness.'
Such were his words; and he left the fields of Galilee
and made for Judea, where the green Jordan silently
breaks through the rich countryside in its pleasant course.
And no less [did he continue] to grant health to the sick lying on their beds,
and he bestows the gifts of the Father on high.
Then the Pharisees came, testing him with a question:
was it lawful for a man to cast off his wife and break the bond
for any cause at all that wounds a husband's heart?
When Christ heard this, he gave this answer:
‘In the beginning God set on the earth a pair of different sexes
and commanded them to be joined as one body,
and the souls of both to grow together in united limbs.
So what God by his own word commands to grow together,
it is unlawful for men to separate through foul lust.
Moses, because he saw how hard their hearts were, commanded
that a writ of divorce be written, so that stony hearts
might be convicted by their own letters under the judging flame.
For whoever rashly dissolves the rights of the chaste bed,
and takes another wife to share his marriage chamber,
will incur the charge of adultery, with the people as witness.’
The disciples reply: ‘This law bears hard on men,
and weighs one party down with an unequal load of servitude,
so that it would be better to do without hateful marriage altogether.’
The Lord answered: ‘Not all will put their shoulders
under so great a weight; such gifts belong to a chosen
virtue. Bodies are cut off in a threefold way,
bodies that take no joy in the begetting law of the marriage bed.
For some, we find, are born such into the shores of light;
many men are stripped of their sex by the force of iron;
and others, it is clear, take away from themselves,
for the kingdom of heaven, the downward-leaning love of the heart.
Whoever is able, let him lay hold with lofty virtue
of the gift that God wills to open to a chosen few.’
So he spoke; and the children whom their parents' glad care
was eagerly bringing from every side with joyful prayers
he took to himself, and the crowd of his followers, because they would forbid them,
he rebuked, and declared that such as these earn the kingdom
of the heavenly court. One by one he laid his holy hands
upon them, and gave them back to their parents' arms to carry.
But see, from the crowd a young man, who had lands and a house
and treasure, a glittering wealth of possessions,
comes up and humbly worships Christ before them all:
‘O good teacher, tell me now, what deeds must I follow
so that I may lay hold of everlasting life?’
To this Jesus, the author of life, then gave this reply:
‘Do you only now ask what the ancient law contains?
You shall not take a man's life, nor stealthily
invade another's bed; nor shall a harmful mind or hand
gather gain from others' goods; you shall not bear false witness.
Let your father and mother be exalted by your honor,
and let your neighbor and brother be to you in love as yourself.’
Then he said: ‘All these I believe I have always kept
with unceasing care; but lest anything perhaps left out
be lacking, let me be counseled by your voice here and now.’
Then Christ says: ‘If now you seek to reach
the perfect heights of life by surpassing merit,
all that you hold alone as your own property
sell, and without a care give it to the wretched poor.
Then you will have treasure stored up in the citadel of heaven,
and, holding fast to virtue, you will follow in our footsteps.’
When these words reached the young man's ears,
he cast down his face and went back sadly to his house.
Then the one hope of life speaks thus to the disciples:
‘It is hard for those fastened to the earth by rich treasure
to be torn away and come, unburdened, into the kingdom of heaven.
For sooner could the huge limbs of the ungainly camel
pass through the narrow eye of a needle
than a rich man could see the heavenly kingdom.’
At these words his companions, astonished and stunned, fell silent,
pondering how great a virtue would have to dwell in the human
heart to be able to lay hold of such a life.
The glory of the everlasting life of the just looked at them
and said: ‘To man these things may perhaps seem harsh,
but for the chosen God lays open into the heavens an easy
and possible way, which lofty virtue may take.’
Then Peter, fortified by the walls of faith, began:
‘We long ago cast aside and left all that was ours,
and our one remaining hope is to follow your commands.
What is left for our souls? Tell us, Christ, we pray.’
Jesus answered Peter with these words:
‘All of you who, believing in the deep recesses of the mind,
keep to my way: when the Son of Man
sits on high, and majesty encircles him
with lofty honor, there a most glorious power
will set up for you twice six seats upon a sublime summit,
and you will likewise be permitted to judge mankind.
Here, whoever leaves the treasures of his own, of his family and his house,
and all his affections for the sake of our name,
shall receive them a hundredfold hereafter, and life everlasting.
The last shall surpass the merit of the first,
and the first, passed over, shall scarcely receive the last rewards.’
‘Like an industrious lord of an estate, whose land
sweet vineyards crown far and wide in rich fields:
he went out at the first light of the sun
and hired the strongest of young men, agreeing
on a fixed wage for a single day's labor,
and then ordered them to dress his vineyards with care.
But going out himself, when the third hour had come,
he found, behold, others, and told them to join the work,
promising fitting rewards for the merit of their labor;
they too gladly followed his instructions.
And when afterward the sixth hour of the day had slipped by,
he went on in just the same way to hire other young men.
And then, when the ninth hour had been driven on by the sun's course,
he likewise hired others and told them to go in.
The last portion of the fading day remained:
going out, he sees young men and asks them the reason
why they lay idle in slow leisure with lazy hands.
They say that no employer had given them
any orders. The lord then told these too
to set to work on his land. But as soon as evening came,
he ordered that all should receive the honor of a wage,
and all carry away their reward in equal coin.
Then that band of men who had taken up their labor at first light
and had borne the whole day in their work
spoke indignantly among themselves, grumbling thus:
“It is unjust that we should get the same coin as these,
whom the last hour joined late to the work.”
Then the lord of the estate speaks with a calm heart:
“Your share of the wage is paid you whole
and untouched, and the terms of a faithful bargain are kept.
Let me be allowed to grant as much from what is mine to these
whom the final portion of the work gathered to the field.”
For holy favor has called many men,
of whom it is fitting to set apart a very small part.’
So he spoke, and made his way again toward Jerusalem, and took his companions
aside, and spoke to them alone along the road:
‘Knowing what awaits us, we go in and approach the savage walls.
Here the Son of Man will be betrayed to the uttermost of death,
bearing in his body the mockery of the scribes and chief men,
and, nailed to the cross, he will rise after the third dawn.’
Then the wife of Zebedee humbly asked
that in the lofty citadel of heaven, with Christ between them,
her blessed sons might sit at his right and left.
Then Christ asks whether they could take up the cup
which by his Father's commands awaited him to take.
Both reply that they can. Then Christ says:
‘It is right for you to drink our cup, but to sit
with me on the lofty seats in equal honor,
that our power will not grant to anyone as a gift.
These lofty gifts the Father reserves for those appointed.’
Then, when all the disciples were stirred up
by these words, he soothes them with such honorable speech:
‘Among the faithless nations, power with lofty dominion
sets over them whoever lord it over them,
and they wreak savage wrath on subject cities.
Among you, far more tranquilly, gentle moderation
smooths the seas of life in harmonious peace,
and the servant grows great above the heights through his services.
No one can be first, the one above all,
unless he serves everyone. So the Son of Man, as your servant,
alone carries out holy duties by his own obedience,
and, redeeming many with his precious blood, saves them.
But you wish to climb higher from the slightest resources,
and so, slipping from the highest, you reach the lowest.’
‘If anyone invites you, setting out the feast of a dinner,
let each who is wise avoid placing himself
on the highest couches. If perhaps another, nobler guest arrives,
he will be shamefully made to give up the place of honor,
the one whom the swelling of a puffed-up heart had set at the top.
But if he is content to take a middling place at the dinner,
then, if a lesser guest soon comes in after him,
he will modestly move up to better places on the couches.’
Then he climbed the heights of the mountain near Jerusalem,
which gleam with rows of grey-leaved olive trees.
From there Christ ordered chosen ones from among the disciples who followed him,
pointing out the dwellings of the village opposite,
to bring from there a she-ass they would find together with her foal
beside her; and if anyone wanted to inquire the reason
why his beasts were so suddenly being led off somewhere,
they were to say that the Lord wished to make use of their service.
The disciples carry out the orders with swift readiness.
They bring them, and spread the soft covering of their garments
over the gentle foal, and offer it for him to sit on.
Of this the herald voice of the ancient prophet once flowed forth:
‘Behold, your gentle king comes to you, whom, as he sits,
the backs of a very meek ass and of the foal following carry.’
Then all the people cover the streets with their garments,
and wherever Christ's way leads, they crown it with strewn branches.
Then others strip the nearby palm groves of their green,
and all shout aloud: ‘To him sprung from David's line,
Hosanna! In the highest be glad glory with triumph!’
Thus, then, Christ enters the walls of Jerusalem.
As he entered, at the very threshold of the temple,
a crowd crippled in legs and eyes ran eagerly to meet him.
When the whole faction of the priests saw them so suddenly
strong in step and sight, they marveled,
and seeing the children filling the temple roofs with the shout
‘Hosanna to him born of David's noble stock,’
they all ask him what cause of shouting
lifts up such a crowd of children in joy.
Christ replied to this: ‘You are believed to know the writings of the holy law,
which say that from the mouth of infants
and from the tongues of sucklings righteous praise arises.’
So he spoke, and leaving the ungrateful city with its citizens
he made for Bethany; and on his return he sees at the edge
of the road a fig tree stretching out its spreading shade.
There, as the desire for food chanced to stir his heart,
he handles the branches of the tree, but no store
of fruit had grown in the barren shade of its leaves.
Christ said to it: ‘May you never have abundance
to bring forth fruit.’ At once the tree withered.
The disciples marvel at the swift death of the tree.
But Christ, standing beside them in their amazement, speaks thus:
‘Now you are amazed that this wood, at our dignity's word,
has ceased to draw earthly sap to give it strength.
But I will tell you with true words again and again:
if sure faith stands firm in the citadel of the mind,
and does not lie trembling, wavering through doubtful failings,
the substance of this tree will yield to us.
And not only this, but the lofty heights of a mountain
can be torn away by the word of believers and buried in the waves of the deep,
together with its forests, rocks and wild beasts.
And whatever faith asks with a sturdy heart,
the worthy virtue of believers will always obtain.’
When he had said this, he went within the walls of the temple.
At once the chief men of the people gathered and asked
what great power had granted these wonders.
Christ said to them: ‘It is easy now to tell you
all that you ask, if your opinion first, in a few words,
will in turn answer what I ask you.
Lately John, who in the pure stream washed away
the stains of a filthy people: did he seem to you divine power,
or rather a human deception?’
So he spoke, hemming in with the double-edged weight of his words
the minds of the chief men who sought to trap him; for the people's
great reverence regarded John as a prophet,
and they could not call his life a deception.
On the other hand, had they said he was a lofty prophet,
the admission would bring on them the guilt of having killed him.
So the deceitful faction answered that they did not know.
Then Christ: ‘It is not unjust for me to withhold my answer,
when the proud chief men withhold their answers from me.’
‘For the father of two sons spoke these words
into the ears of the elder: “The greater part of my vineyard
lies half-pruned. Go, then, and with strong vigor,
working now with the spade, now with the pruning hook, cut back the vines.”
Then the young man says he will not put up with such squalid
talk of labor. Afterward he carries out all his father's orders
and, condemning himself, takes back his reply.
Then he bade the other son in similar words
to spend the labor he was bidden on his vineyards.
The young man agreed to this, but did not match his words with deeds.
Tell me, which of them rather follows his father's orders?’
They commend the later response.
Christ goes on: ‘Now mark these true words.
Those who seek sordid gain from the vices of the body
can henceforth more readily lay hold of the seat of heaven
than any of you. For righteous John had come to you
before, but it is not your way to believe.
The hearts of harlots, rather, drank in sure faith
and put away the shameful filth of the soul.
But you never repent at all of such great crimes.’
‘So a certain rich man, whose many acres of gleaming
vineyard a thick hedge encloses all around,
built in the middle a tower, a winepress and vats,
and handed it over to tenants and leased out the fruits for them to hold,
setting the terms for paying the rent laid on them.
Then he goes to far-off lands; but at the set time of the harvest
he sends servants as his agents, to whom the tenants
should hand over his share intact, the fixed rent of the land.
But see, the frenzy of the tenants drives these off with savage blows,
and others with volleys of stones from every side;
at last they lay many low with deadly wounds.
Then the lord of the land orders more servants to go
and once more demands the rent agreed;
but against the many a greater, bolder outrage rises.
At last the lord resolves to send his son,
because the due force of respect demanded that his offspring,
a part of himself, should be revered in the tenants' hearts.
But they, on the contrary, their minds already stained with blood,
believing that once the lord's offspring was destroyed
the lordship would afterward pass to them, pierce him with a cruel wound,
cut him down, and throw his corpse out beyond the hedge.
After this the lord will come and exact punishment
for such great crimes. But the seat of the shining kingdom,
once given to you, will be taken away and carried over
to a peaceable nation that can render its fruits.’
‘Like a king who, joining his son in the bonds of marriage,
orders the nobles to throng the joyful banquet,
summoning them through his servants to celebrate together
the honor of the royal wish; but all refuse to come
to the royal wedding and the cups of the royal table.
Afterward he sends others to say that he has prepared
everything most lavishly, splendid dishes and a joyful feast.
But they, disregarding his bounty, went off in different directions.
One went back to his own house, another to the dwelling of his nearby farm,
another to his wares and gains instead.
Many, moreover, seize the innocent servants
sent to call them to the festivities, and torture their bodies
with the sword to death. Then, when the king learned what had been done,
with thousands of armed men he overthrew the citizens
together with their very walls, avenging his servants' shed blood.
Then he says to his servants: “The wedding feast,
all that we furnished with most lavish wealth,
those nobles have scorned to touch at my tables.
Go therefore quickly through the public ways of the streets,
and whomever chance has gathered there, call them all
and bring them here to my son's joyful wedding.”
The servants went out through all the crossroads of the streets
and brought together those they found. At last all
the tables are filled with a mixed crowd of no name.
There the just and the unjust, being called, reclined together.
But the king came in and looked over the joyful banquet.
There he sees a man dressed in a defiled garment,
whose speech had been out of tune with the joys of the wedding.
And when the weight of the royal word bids him
give reasons for the stains and the soiling of his garment,
he fell silent, the mouth of his impure heart stopped.
And then the king, turning, orders the servants
to bind him hand and foot and his whole body,
seize him, and at once hurl him into the deep darkness.
There will be the gnashing of vast pain without end,
and weeping forever. For though many are often called,
a blessed choice of few men will be made.’
BOOK FOUR.
As he said this, the faction at once, gnashing their teeth,
set out to test him with deceitful and malicious words:
"It is certain that you have now come as a truthful teacher,
and, fearing no one, you keep to the footsteps of the Lord.
Tell us, then, whether it is lawful for our nation to pay
tribute under the law of Caesar, who presses on us always?"
But he, seeing into the depths of their cruel hearts, said:
"Why do you try now to trap me with words,
you deceivers? The deceit of the mind betrays its fruit.
Look at a coin, at the bronze of the stamped piece,
where it is easy to see Caesar's face impressed.
Pay him now the tribute under his own law,
and let us keep for God the honor that is his by law."
After this the Sadducees pressed him from every side with their barking:
"Moses, who laid down the precepts of the law, commanded
that if anyone leaves his marriage through an early death,
with no children yet born of his seed between them,
the bond of union is owed in turn to his brother,
so that no part of the fallen family should perish.
In our country there were seven brothers;
the eldest was the first to take on the bonds of a bride,
and soon fell under the swift blade of death.
Then another brother, in the same fruitless marriage bed,
died, and all the brothers lay dead, one after another.
And all of them were mourned with the tears of the one wife;
afterward the harshness of chill death snatched her too.
If, then, they all come to the threshold of life,
to whose marriage will the woman rise to be restored?"
Christ said to them: "Bound by a perverse error,
your hard mind resists the laws and commands of the Lord.
For the second restoration of joyful life hereafter
knows no marriage beds, nor the empty joys of earth;
rather, like the nimble ministers beside the Father,
the sublime power of the kingdom will set them in its hall.
Nor does God choose to make himself the Lord of those
who, sinking down, have deserved to meet a foul death,
but rather of those who can lay hold of the light of life."
See, others ask him what are the firmest points of the law.
He, untiring, denied an answer to no one:
"Let the devotion of the heart love the Lord exalted in heaven;
this is the firmest strength of the law.
Like it is this: let the inmost places of a just mind
be held by great love to what is owed a brother;
for on these twin commands all things depend.
But whose offspring do you think he will be,
the Christ whom all the prophets promise through the ages?"
They answer that he is born of David's line.
Christ goes on: "Why is it written that David,
by the divine breath, calls him both Lord and God,
when it is not fitting for a father to say this of his own son?"
So spoke the Savior; all were astonished and fell silent.
But he called the crowd of believers to him and spoke out:
"Look at the scribes, proud on their lofty seat.
Whatever they teach, it is right to take in with the heart's
obedience; but despise the stains of their life.
For they lay crushing burdens on your shoulders
which they themselves will not touch even with a finger.
By the first place at dinner, by arrogant pride,
and by the empty honor of those who greet them they are puffed up,
and they want to bear the lofty title of teacher.
But I would not have you aspire to the height of a lofty name;
for you the authority of a single teacher
has been imposed forever by the law of heaven,
and that same law has joined you in equal love as brothers.
Likewise there is one Father, who reigns at the summit of heaven.
If anyone among you lifts his neck on high,
he will fall and be plunged into the lowest mire of the abyss;
but the humble man will climb freely into the bright sky.
Ever to be wept for are the scribes, and, in this tearful age,
the blind deceit of the Pharisees' crowd, to be lamented by all.
For since the way is closed to you, and rightly denied,
you let no one else enter the heights of light,
and you drag everyone into fellowship with the cruel flame.
I would call you like tombs covered with splendor,
whose face is gleaming, but whose graves are foul within.
So your voice is veiled under the semblance of a just life,
and filthy hearts are hidden in the recesses of the mind."
"O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who so often with the sword
have endlessly slain the prophets sent for your life,
how I longed to protect your nation and your people,
as a bird is wont to cherish her sweet chicks beneath her body,
embracing them all round with the shelter of her wings!
But to you heavenly gifts are always worthless.
Now already this house is forsaken, to be laid waste in ruins,
and it is no longer permitted you to see our face."
He goes out of the temple, and as they gazed at its lofty
walls, he taught the disciples with these words:
"These marvels of workmanship seem to you worthy
of an astonished gaze; but learn from true words
that soon all of it will lie scattered everywhere on the ground."
Saying this, he had reached the height of Olivet.
When the disciples saw him alone, they asked him
to set out for them the time of the age to come,
what end his promises were to reach,
and when his coming would consume the globe of the earth.
To the words of those asking, Christ answered thus:
"Beware of deceit, lest your credulity, caught by a false name,
be cast headlong into the snares of those who stray.
The fires of war will run through every land;
but stand firm with mighty strength of heart,
lest your mind lie confounded by the tumult it hears of,
for the first battles will not bring the end so soon.
Nations against nations and kings against kings
will bear their standards; nor will diseases then spare to corrupt the expanse
of the air, nor plagues to lay bodies low.
Even the earth, fixed with solid weight in the void,
will tremble in various places with a shaking motion.
These will be but small trials at the beginning.
Many of you will be betrayed and handed over to death,
and for my name the nations must fall upon you
with torments, savage punishments, and hatred.
There will be envy on earth, all things will be full of errors,
and false prophets will arise to the ruin of the peoples.
Amid all this, if anyone can keep his breast protected from wounds
to the end, he will enter the heights of light,
crowned with the eternal garlands of life.
The proclamation of the kingdom of heaven will fly
to all the bounds of the earth; every nation will have
a witness in the light-streaming word of holy salvation.
And then will come the end, dissolving the running ages.
Then a grievous desolation will come upon the earth,
which has as its warrant the most true voice of Daniel;
only a worthy reader will be able to understand this.
Let the Jews flee far away and take to the mountains,
and let no one go back to his house to take with him
anything to accompany his flight, a garment or any movable thing.
Pitiable then will be mothers with the burden of the womb,
and those who will nourish their wretched infants with sweet milk.
Ask even now in prayer that your flight may not come
in the cold of grim winter, nor that wavering fear
disturb the festal sabbath with headlong running;
for the cruelest burdens will come upon all lands.
Such evil no ages before have known, nor will any after.
And unless the exalted Father, in pity, were willing to cut short the time
and shorten the number of the days,
no bodies would thereafter survive of all fearful life.
But for the sake of the chosen just, mercy will come.
Deceivers in the name of Christ and false prophets
will rise up on earth and fashion mighty portents,
marvels that may perhaps ensnare even the chosen just.
See, the ages to come lie open to you, foretold.
If anyone says that Christ is roaming the deserts
or is stored away far off in hidden chambers,
let such utterly empty credulity be far from you.
For as the lightning runs across the open sky
and is easily seen by all, from the shores of the east
to the west, where the sky sinks to its rim,
so with a swift coming will the lights of Christ shine forth.
The sun will hide his ruddy rays in dark shadows,
the grace of the moon's light will lose its course,
and the fire-haired stars will fall and leave the sky.
Likewise every power of the heaven above, shaken,
will give signs by which the Son of Man may shine
at the height of heaven; and unending lamentation will press upon
all the tribes, when with fire-colored clouds
the Son of Man will come through the stars, mighty in majesty.
Then the trumpet, blaring with terrifying clangor, will gather
the called and just from the four quarters of the world.
For the present generation of this age will not pass away
until the end that follows closes all that is owed to it.
This earth and the heaven above will dissolve into fire,
but my words will never be dissolved from their order.
What that day will be, it is right that no one should know,
except only the Lord of all things, who turns the stars.
As once the raging waters engulfed the lands,
and, while all were busy at their various tasks,
the violence of the flood swept them off in a sudden rush,
so suddenly, rolling flames, our coming will descend
from the sky; nor will it bear down on all under one
condition. For then, where two are cleaving the glad acres
into furrows beneath the pressed-down plow,
one ploughman will be taken, his body snatched up,
and the other, unaware, will be left in the wide field.
Indeed, even those lying on the straw of one bed
will undergo different judgments by a differing lot.
For one, left behind, will search for his companion across the bedding.
Therefore let the servants keep watch, because, unknown to them,
the coming of the Lord will descend at a sudden hour.
If every keeper of a house knew the certain time
when the thief would come upon him, he would keep watch and bear arms
against him from afar, lest anyone break in and enter the house.
But you must always stand ready with attentive minds,
for suddenly and unexpectedly the Son of Man will return
here to you, keeping for the just their rewards.
That servant will be faithful to whom the man, the father of the house himself,
setting out on a long journey, chose to entrust his whole house and servants:
wise is he and blessed beyond measure
whom the Lord at his coming will find keeping his commands.
He will crown that servant with greater honor.
But that wretch who, reveling in filth,
despises his delaying master, wears out his fellow servants
with blows, indulges in sluggish drunkenness,
and has thronged the banquets of the dissolute —
the master will come, and the servant raging heedlessly
he will hurl headlong and bury in the ruin of deserved punishment.
Everlasting weeping and gnashing of teeth will await him."
"The heavenly kingdom can be compared to ten maidens,
one part of whom was wiser,
the other part most foolish, with dull hearts.
They all went out to meet the bridal rites,
equipped with the adornment of flame-haired torches.
But the wise part, so that their lights might keep their flame,
took care to carry oil with them as well.
The foolish had no such prudence.
And as the bridegroom delayed, their limbs were loosed in sleep,
all of them, along the broad crossroads.
Now at midnight a great cry arises and swells,
and bids them go out to meet the joyful wedding
and adorn the roads with gleaming torches.
The maidens hastened to rise, to furnish their torches with light,
and to trim the flames with rich oil.
Then the foolish ask that a share of the oil be given them,
which they saw the prudent were carrying with them.
But since the wise company fears that, for all alike,
the rich nourishment of the bright flame would run short
if from so little an equal share were given to all,
the foolish then go off to buy liquid oil.
While they are gone, the joyful procession passes through everything,
and only the prudent band accompanies the bridegroom.
The dull ones arrive, sluggish, long afterward,
and knock at the bridegroom's doors and the closed threshold
again and again in vain, and ply him with unwelcome prayers
that the wretched women be allowed to enter the joyful threshold.
None of the bridegroom's companions was willing to know them,
nor was the bridegroom himself. Keep watch, then, in fear,
since the hour of the coming is not certain to you."
"For it is like a man who happened to set out
for far-off lands, and, entrusting talents to his servants to manage,
gave five to one, while another received two to hold,
and a third took on the care of managing one talent,
since differing abilities deserve differing things.
Those to whom the greater portion of money was entrusted
eagerly increased it with twofold gains.
But he to whom the care of one talent was entrusted
buries it in the ground and keeps the money without fruit.
And now the master was back: then the first and the second
show him that they have doubled what was entrusted to them.
The master praises them and promises to entrust greater things
to such faithfulness. But the third digs up
the talent and returns it to his master with these words:
'Since I knew that I served a harsh master,
who reaps crops grown from another's seed,
I was afraid, and preferred to entrust your silver to the earth,
so that I could always return it to you safe.'
Then the master answers the servant, beginning thus:
'If you dared to say you did not know my ways,
I could grant pardon for such great worthlessness.
But knowing them, you ought all the more to have seen to it
that the money, put to work, would bring us a return.
Therefore let our portion be taken from the sluggard
and a greater holding now be given to the prudent one
whom I found to have heaped up my five talents with twofold gain.
For it is certain that those deserve greater things
whose wealth abounds more richly in an increased share.
But he who has small means, with a sluggish heart,
will justly have even that little taken from him entirely,
so that the worthless servant, plunged into the deepest darkness,
may keep up endless weeping with the gnashing of punishment.'"
"See, the Son of Man will come and, attended by his Father's ministers,
will sit as judge upon a lofty seat.
Then all the nations from the different parts of the world
will gather, and he will separate all the just from the taint of the wicked
and gladly place them on the right side,
but the depraved, scorned, he will leave on the left side;
as a shepherd divides the pasture of a mixed flock,
granting the woolly sheep the soft grass of the right-hand meadow,
but leaving the shaggy goats on the left to crop the thornbushes.
Then the king, turning to those on the right, will say:
'Come here, you holy ones, receive the long-owed gifts
of the Father, which are as old as the shining world
and were prepared and promised to the just from its first beginning.
For once, when I was weary with hunger, these kindly people refreshed me,
and often relieved my thirst with drink;
the hospitality of a home often opened to me when I was invited,
and when naked I received the most welcome covering of clothes,
and in the pains of prison I received their comfort.'
Then the blessed answer the Lord with these words:
'None of us remembers seeing you naked,
or noticed you crushed under the harsh rule of hunger,
or remembers seeing you bound in the pains of prison.'
Then the judge will answer them thus:
'Whoever has done these things for my brothers, pitying their lowly hardships,
has surely set sweet fruit before me.'
'But you, unjust ones, go into the just flames,
and roast your malicious minds forever in torments,
which the Father prepared in the dreadful, deep pools of the abyss
for the companions of the dreadful demon and for himself.
For once, when I suffered thirst, no cups,
nor, in the pain of hunger, the mercy of a little bread,
nor, when I was a stranger, the covering of roof or clothing,
were ever given me even briefly, a slender share of your great wealth;
nor, when I was shut in behind prison bars or lay sick,
was there ever the comfort of your visit.'
Then the condemned band will reply with these words:
'None of us ever remembers seeing you
sick and enduring the hardship of thirst or savage hunger,
or wandering as a stranger through the towns in weary want,
or sunk in the pains of prison, or weighed down by sickness,
so that just pity might have been shown you in your distress.'
To them the Lord of all things will say: 'When your savagery
swelled in your proud hearts against those in straitened circumstances
and trampled on the humble and the least, it scorned me in them.'
When he has spoken these words, he will render to merits their rewards.
The wretched wicked will be pierced with punishment forever,
and the salvation granted to the just will endure forever."
While he speaks these things, a sister, her hair torn and disheveled,
anxious with rightful care over her brother's sickness,
urges a young man to run over with swift steps,
so that Christ might save his friend from such great misfortune.
For the woman had won favor by her kindly merits,
and for her devoted service Christ embraced her brother and her deserving household
and held them in full love.
The messenger arrives and reports that, at the last extremity,
the young man dear to Christ lay in the sorrows of sickness,
holding the uttermost border between death and life.
His name was Lazarus. But Christ, struck by the bitter words, said:
"This violence of sickness, if you believe,
does not lead to death,
but is so that God may be celebrated by the just with due honor
and the Son of Man may shine with holy power."
Then to the disciples: "Lazarus now sleeps," he said,
"but I will make the dear young man rise again."
The disciples say: "After sleep full health
can return"; nor did they grasp in their minds
that Christ had spoken of death under the name of sleep.
He removed their error with these words:
"Lazarus has fallen into death; but joy comes to my mind
from this, and it arms your faith in me more strongly,
since you see that, though far away, I behold all things.
But let us make haste," he said. Then Didymus speaks thus:
"Let us go, and let us all alike be forced to fall in death,
as the Jewish nation so often threatens."
And now Christ was at hand; but it happened to be the fourth day
since the burial, and grief and the tearful house held
the sisters, plunged by death into black darkness.
There, giving due consolation, had gathered
the leading men of the Jewish nation and dear kinsfolk.
But Martha, hearing that Christ had come, ran
to meet him, leaving the house and her grieving sister,
and cried from afar: "O if only your power had been here
with us and had snatched our brother from bitter death!
For whatever you ask, it is certain that it can be granted you."
The Lord consoles her in her groaning with these words:
"Take courage, woman, and recover a steadfast mind.
This Lazarus will rise again into the light of life."
And the woman: "Surely all mortals will rise to the gifts of life
when the end comes to the world."
Christ in turn brings forth these words from his holy breast:
"Behold, I am for you the restoration of bright life.
Whoever believes in me will be able to lay aside the death he has incurred
and join his life to the unending age.
And whoever takes up faith in a living heart
will never reach the dreadful threshold of death.
Do you believe this from a pure heart, Martha?"
She then: "This one faith will hold my heart:
that in you has come, worthy of worship, the heavenly offspring
of God on high, under the exalted name of Christ."
So she spoke and, to stir her sister Mary to come running,
went inside; she told her that the holy master had come
and was calling for her, her sister, weighed down like her with grief,
signaling it all with a silent nod.
Mary leaps out of doors on hearing the name of Christ;
and with her, as she groans, follows a crowd from Jerusalem,
believing that the sisters were taking their weeping to the tomb.
When she saw Jesus, the bringer of salvation,
she fell before his feet and burst out with this cry:
"If you could have seen my brother while he was alive,
Lazarus could never have succumbed to cruel death."
Christ, joining heartfelt grief to these tears,
asks where the tomb is, in which had lately been laid
the limbs robbed of the warmth of the winged soul.
Without delay they show the weeping, sorrowful Lord the sepulchre
beneath a hewn rock; when the Holy One saw it closed
by the weight of a stone, he orders it moved at once with many levers;
but Martha's voice strikes the air with these words:
"See, four days and as many nights in turn
have passed since his limbs were laid to rest in the ground.
I would think that the body, now that the stir of warmth has fled,
gives off a wretched stench from its decaying limbs."
To these words Christ replies thus:
"It has been said so often already that, in great matters, faith
stands by the strength of those who believe; but the glory of the most high
Father is now at hand, if you have the strength of faith."
When he had said this, and the huge rock, its barriers pulled away,
lay open, that power, knowing what it was, soon lifted its gaze to heaven
and prayed to the Father with these words:
"Exceeding thanks, holy Father, we confess to you;
you always hear me graciously with your venerable ears,
but let the people here learn to believe that I was sent."
When he had said this, he stood at once on the very threshold of the tomb,
filling the hollow rocks with a cry aimed straight at them:
"Lazarus, receive into your slumbering limbs your soul as it returns —
behold it! — and come forth yourself out of the tomb."
Without delay, his hands and feet bound, he suddenly
comes out of the tomb, his face wrapped in woven linen,
and a thin band binding his whole body.
Then Jesus ordered him unbound and sends him home rejoicing.
When the Jews saw this venerable deed,
those who had followed Mary and Martha in such numbers,
some, believing, follow and honor such great power;
but others head back to the city, and to the proud Pharisees
among the leaders they recount all the wonders of the event.
So the scribes are summoned to council, and with them a weightier number
of the people, where on high shine the beautiful halls
of the seat of Caiaphas, chief of the priests.
There they resolved to lay Christ low in death,
but to avoid the days of Passover, lest, with the crowds thronging,
the divided people should be swept by fury into war.
He was at the house of Simon, from whom livid leprosy
had fled by his power. See, as he reclined at table,
a woman comes close and, from an alabaster jar
holding precious ointments of widely fragrant oil,
pours it over holy Christ from the top of his head.
The disciples rebuke her, saying that the bodies of the wretched poor
could have been helped by the price of the ointment.
The Lord forbids these words and approved the deed:
"Stop hindering this righteous girl in her devotion.
There will always be time to come to the aid of the poor,
but you will not always be granted to see me.
She performs this most praiseworthy service
for my burial, and such deeds will fill the world."
Then one of the disciples, Judas, out of his mind,
slips away and ran to the leaders with these words:
"What price may I hope for, if I can betray to you
and point out the master you have long been seeking?"
At once they fix the sum at thirty weights
of silver; for these Judas gave himself up to deep crime.
And now the day of Passover had advanced from its first dawn:
the disciples ask where he wished to eat the Passover supper;
and he bade them seek out a certain man, unnamed,
who would receive the master's final instructions.
Soon, at early evening, as the twelve disciples reclined together
at table, the master prophesied with these words:
"See, the time is pressing, when one of you
is turning over in his wicked heart how to betray Christ to death."
At once they all ask who, daring such a thing,
had taken so great a poison into his mad heart.
He then said: "He is eating at the feast with me now.
The Son of Man will indeed undergo the punishments long ago foretold
in due time. But wretched forever is he
who hands over the just one; how much happier he would be
if he had never touched the light of life on earth!"
And Judas, heavily burdened in his guilty breast,
said: "Surely such suspicion does not touch Judas?"
The Lord answered: "I see that it is you who say so."
When he had said this, he broke bread with his hands,
then gives it out, divided, and having prayed in holiness,
taught the disciples that in this way they eat his own body.
Then the Lord takes the cup and, when it was filled with wine,
sanctifies it with words of thanksgiving and gives them to drink,
and taught them that he had shared out his own blood,
and said: "This blood has redeemed the sins of the people;
drink this, my blood. For believe my true words:
after this I will never taste the juice of the vine
until the kingdom of the Father, by the gift of a better life,
grants me to rise again to new wine."
Then, when a hymn had been sung in holy harmony,
they all climb the heights of the Mount of Olives.
Then Christ brings forth these words from his breast:
"All of you, in this present hour of night,
wretched terror will scatter far and wide, your leader forsaken.
For so it is written: At the shepherd's fall, all
the sheep will scatter in flight every way across the fields.'
'But afterward, when life gives back to me the new honours of heaven,
I will go before you, and in my native fields,
moving through the welcome countryside of Galilee, I will teach your company.'
Peter answered: 'Even if it is right to believe that all the rest
might waver and deny your teachings,
no misfortune will ever change my heart.'
He replied: 'This night, which brings the bright stars over the earth
and now, pressing down the light, broods over the waves,
will hear you, in your fear, speak lies three times over
and deny Christ, most valiant Peter,
and that before the roofs of the houses ring with the cry of birds.'
But Peter said: 'I would rather suffer a cruel death
than that this voice should forget and deny its master.'
All of them persisted in promising the same strength of heart.
There is a place whose fields bear the Hebrew name Gethsemane.
There the author of light and life went on his way,
and his disciples followed around him, Judas having fled.
There he ordered the rest of his followers to sit down,
while he himself took Peter to go on far ahead with him,
together with the sons of Zebedee, and made his way through the lonely paths.
Then, sorrowful with heavy anguish, he spoke these words:
'My soul, now turning over grievous things, troubles my heart
even to death; but now shut out sluggish sleep,
and spend this anxious night with me in watching.'
So he spoke, and going on a little, he pressed his body to the earth
and, lying prostrate, prayed in these words:
'If it may be, Father, let the violence of this cup,
bearing down on me with its powerful pull, pass me by.
Yet rather let your will be done than mine,
the judgement you have decreed in matters so great.'
Then he went back to the disciples, but sleep had overcome them all
as they lay stretched on the ground, their limbs heaving with heavy breath.
Then he said to Peter: 'Have you not the strength to give me
a single hour of watching amid such great dangers?
Watch, I pray you, lest dreadful temptation seize you
and hurl you headlong down the slippery path of cruel death.
The spirit is strong, but the body is weak and falters.'
Again he withdrew to the height of the secluded mountain
and prayed to the Father: 'Most gentle ruler of all things,
