since it is not possible for this cup to pass,
let your will now be done concerning my lot.'
Again he found the disciples weighed down by sleep,
and having once more prayed the same prayer to the Father,
he spoke to them as they lay bound in the weary languor of rest:
'Now you may sleep and go back to your companions,
for look, he is coming who will hand over my body to all
that a defiled faction will inflict upon my limbs.'
As he spoke, Judas arrived with a great throng of men crowding about him,
sent at the command of the leaders and the fierce people.
Some with drawn swords, some trusting in the weight of their clubs,
were following the sign that raging Judas had promised.
For he had agreed that he would touch Christ with a kiss,
so that the wretched mob might easily seize the man they did not know.
When he, dissembling, greeted him in a coaxing voice
and touched with his lips the venerable face of the Just One,
at once Christ said: 'You may carry it all through,
whatever the reason you have come here so prepared.'
The crowd laid hands on him and seized Christ.
Then one of the disciples, with flashing sword,
rushed in rage upon the high priest's servant
and with the force of the blow struck the ear from his temple.
Christ said to him: 'Put down your sword, my friend;
for whoever fiercely trusts in an avenging blade,
a like vengeance of the blade will justly await him.
Or could I not summon the hosts of heaven
and lead my Father's countless squadrons into battle?
But the scripture must be fulfilled, as is due, in what befalls me.
But you who rush together to seize me with drawn steel,
with clubs and swords — see, I
come out to meet you, I who always sat in the midst of the temple's height
among you and taught, and no one ever dared such things
against me alone, though so many were barking all around me.'
The disciples fled in all directions, abandoning Christ.
And now the Saviour stood in the hall of Caiaphas,
when all the scribes and the summoned leaders came.
But Peter, alone, following his steps from afar,
sat in secret sorrow among the servants,
awaiting the final outcome amid so great a storm.
See, the priests set about seeking false witnesses
and want to weave together invented charges
by which they could impose death on the innocent Christ.
But none seemed enough for such great fury.
At last witnesses sprang forward who said they had heard Jesus
say that he alone could overturn the temple
and, once overturned, raise it up again in three days.
The chief of the priests himself pressed hard upon the silent one,
gnashing his teeth in fury, and spoke these words:
'Why do you not dare to answer anything to such grave charges,
convicted as you are by true witnesses before the leaders?
Yet I will adjure you by the realms of the highest Thunderer
to confess openly whether it is right to believe you are the Christ.'
Then he addressed the proud man in these words:
'These words alone come forth true
from your breast; you will see coming through the air
the majesty of the Son of Man, when at the right hand of holy
Power he sits beneath fire-coloured clouds.'
Hearing this, the priest tore the garment from his breast,
exulting in his fury and blind of heart,
and said: 'You have heard the foul words of a profane man fighting
against God; let our defiled religion rise all the more in wrath,
and all of you now declare your judgement.'
All cried out together and vied to sentence him to death.
Then shameless spittle covered the holy face of Christ,
and slaps on his cheeks and many blows on his head
assailed him, and all vied to mock him with words:
'Prophesy, Christ, whose hand it was that struck you!'
But a woman, because she had seen Peter sitting sad inside,
said: 'Were you too, young man, one of the companions
of this man, whom the leaders' sentence condemns in mockery?'
He denied it and tried to get out of that cruel house.
But see, as he went out, another woman, spotting him at the outer doorway,
betrayed him to the servants with similar words.
Again he spoke, and with an oath denied that he knew him.
Then many came up after them to question him
and said they recognized him from the sound of his voice,
since every word he spoke rang with Galilean speech.
And Peter, swearing to it all with words of cursing,
declared, denying, that he did not know whoever that man was.
Upon these words a bird, beating its wings beneath the ridge of the roof,
followed with its song, and around Simon's sorrowful mind
stood the foretelling words of Christ;
and going out from there he gave way to bitter weeping.
Now the stars were yielding to the light, and the swift sun
came forth, filling the trembling lands with its rays.
And now they dragged Christ from the council, his hands bound behind his back,
into the governor's presence with a great clamour.
Meanwhile the Lord, standing before the lofty tribunal —
Jesus — was met with these words of Pilate:
'Do you stand here as king of the Jewish nation, as is said?'
Christ answered: 'I hear this in your own words.'
Thereupon a terrible accusation rose up against the Just One
and roared, and wicked eloquence pressed hard upon the Holy One.
Jesus did not deign to answer those savage men.
Pilate asked what reason he had for his silence.
He, persisting all the more, kept a wondrous silence.
Now on the solemn feast day the laws, as it happened,
commanded by custom that one man condemned to death be released;
and there was in chains a robber of notorious name,
whom the people, hostile to Christ, were burning to release to life;
but, terrified in her sleep by savage visions,
Pilate's wife, that he should keep clear of punishing the Just One,
anxiously begged her husband with messages and pleas.
Then the judge tried once more to search out the mind of the leaders,
and asked whom they wished to be freed from the impending punishment
and released by law at the people's choice.
But the leaders, canvassing on every side, urged the people
to ask for the robber by the law and to refuse Christ.
And after the leaders' opinion had inflamed the mob,
and it asked rather that the robber's life be granted to it,
the governor asked the people what they wanted done with Jesus.
The people, inflamed with evil, stirred up savage tumults,
and again and again they demanded the punishment of the cross
for one who desired the name of king, who, by confessing himself Caesar's enemy,
had condemned himself with his own mouth.
At last, overcome by force, and loathing the bloody
duty, he protested that he kept his heart free
of this blood, and before them he washed his hands of the crime,
so that the stain might rest on the nation alone.
At this they cried out the more: 'Let this blood follow us, us,
and let this crime and guilt overflow onto our race.'
Pilate granted Barabbas to the people and the law,
and, defeated, handed Jesus over to the punishment of the cross.
But Judas the traitor, when he saw that in his frenzy,
having taken the price of the crime, he had given such a sign,
wretched man, condemning his deeds with true laments,
in loathing flung the silver into the temple.
And setting out to exact his own punishment with a noose,
he seized a hideous death from the top of a fig tree.
Then the priests, since it was the price of blood,
declaring it unlawful to place it in the sanctuary of the temple —
though they had believed it lawful to pay it when blood was being sold —
bought a field, under the true name
of Blood, and so marked their impious crimes with a horrid deed.
This the true voice of the prophet, singing once in veiled words,
had revealed: the outcome of events in the order of the ages.
The profane men fixed thirty minas of silver,
setting this as the price of a precious body,
which soon is passed on to the potter's little field.
(The Just One was handed over to the savage servants of crime,
the soldiers; he offers his body to their wicked mockeries.
They put on him a purple tunic and a scarlet cloak
and wreathed his head with bloody thorns,
and in place of a sceptre a reed was set in his right hand.
Then, kneeling, they hailed him as king and lord
of the Jewish nation, and bathed his face with spittle,
and made sport of his holy head with wicked blows.
When the mad soldiery had finished this mockery,
they led him away clothed again in his own garment
and dragged the holy and just one to the punishment of the cross.
But see, as they went out, they seized a certain Simon,
a native of Cyrene, and ordered him to carry the wood
on which the unchanging order of the ages, pressing on,
urged that the Lord of light be fastened by cruel commands.
And when they came to the place in the country called Golgotha,
they gave Christ cups of wine mixed with gall.
But he, having touched it with the tip of his tongue, refused it,
so that by such things the ancient sayings might be fulfilled,
and yet the mocking rage of men should not have all it demanded.
And now his body hung fixed on the tree of the cross,
and the lot, cast among them all, gave possession of the seamless tunic
to a single soldier, keeping its weave whole.
And they set up a written notice of his charge and offence:
that he had been king of the Jewish people and nation.
It happened that two robbers, one on either side,
shared his punishment with him; but the blind madness of the raging
people jeered at Christ as he hung there:
'This is the one who alone could destroy the temple,
this is the one who could restore it in three courses of the light.
Now let the venerable offspring of the Thunderer come down
and free his body and soul from the punishment of the cross.'
The leaders took up these words of the senseless mob,
and the Pharisees and scribes and the mad faction
mocked him, and wagged their heads and their tongues in insane talk,
to their own binding in eternal punishment:
'Did he not once save others from the cruel bonds
of disease? Why can he not free himself
from punishment? Look, the one we were meant to believe
king of our nation: let him free his body from the timber of the cross!
Then we may rightly believe in his holy signs.
He trusts in God his Father: why does that venerable Power
not wish to release its own Son from punishment?'
No less did the robbers, groaning on the right and on the left,
fastened to crosses as the lot of their crimes, revile him.
Now the course of the light had climbed to the midpoint of its circle,
when suddenly the sun fled from sight, and clothed in dusky darkness
it hid the trembling day in night.
But when, in its disturbance, it had passed the ninth hour,
the dismayed light returned to its world.
And Christ called on his Father with a loud voice
in the manner of the Hebrew tongue; but the ignorant people
thought he was calling Elijah. Then one man, rushing up,
with a foul sponge bound to a reed
pressed it to his lips and forced him to drink its sour taste.
The rest of the raging crowd cackled with these words:
'Let us all watch, in case Elijah, sent back from heaven,
who rests on his lofty seat, should come
and free the king nailed to this wretched stake.'
Then the Lord's cry, sent forth with a great effort,
mingled his soul, its companion, with the airs of heaven.
At that moment the veils of the holy temple were torn,
and the linen, rent into two parts, gaped open,
and the trembling earth was shaken through all its mass,
and rocks burst and split apart from their own bulk.
Then the tombs of men of old lay open, their barriers
thrust back, and righteous souls returned into their bodies
and, [?] here and there among the people, far and wide through the walls
of the city they wandered: so did all things terrify the world.
The hearts of the soldiers were the first to be shaken with fear,
those who were guarding the bodies given over to cruel punishment,
and they called him the Son of God and confessed him the Christ.
From a distance the women watched these great wonders,
all those who used to minister to Christ.)
Now evening had begun to follow the departing sun,
when one alone of the leaders, a more righteous man, dared
to ask for the body of Christ to pay it the last rites.
He bore the name of Joseph, from Arimathea,
and had once lent his ears to the words of Jesus.
He then asked Pilate to grant him the limbs
from which the dreadful force of punishment had just taken life.
The governor granted it, and shining linen
cloths wrapped the body, and it was laid in a new cave of rock.
A huge rolling stone closed the entrance;
from a distance the women kept watch and saw everything.
And now the day was filling the earth with ruddy light,
the day which by ancient law always commanded rest,
but the relentless fury of the leaders kept no rest.
They gathered and burdened the judge's ears with these words:
'A most just punishment has undone the snares of error.
Now it is fitting to remember that this deceiver used
always to boast and promise to the common people
that from the darkness of death to the light of life
he would return when the sun had come round three times.
This we ask: let a guard of soldiers watch over the fresh burial,
lest the wild daring of his disciples to steal the body
should rise up, and a new madness disturb the people.'
And Pilate replied: 'Soldiers are permitted,' he said,
'to guard, as you wish, the body buried in the earth.'
They gathered and rolled the huge weight of the stone,
and guarded the entrance with seals and the stone with soldiers.
Now the stars of night were beginning to yield to the coming sun;
then the women hurried together to visit the enclosure of the tomb,
but at once an earthquake shook the whole earth,
and gliding down from the opened heaven a messenger descended
and rolled the stone away from the entrance of the tomb.
His face shone like the fire of lightning,
and his garments gleamed white as snow.
Terror had shut off all the soldiers' senses,
and they lay together like corpses struck down by death.
But he spoke to the women in these words:
'Let no fear now shake and trouble your hearts;
for it is plain that you seek the holy body
which wicked madness fixed on the wood of the cross.
Christ has risen, and the eternal light of life
he has received in his holy body, having conquered death.
Now you may see that here in the resting place of the tomb
there lie none of the limbs that had been laid in it.
Go back, moreover, swiftly and in haste, and tell
the disciples that Christ has returned to the shores of light
and goes joyfully before them into the land of Galilee.'
At these words and sights a burning joy had flooded
their astonished hearts, along with amazement and wavering fear.
Then, celebrating their joy as they ran headlong,
they left the tomb and brought this news to the disciples.
See, in the middle of the road Jesus showed himself in glory
and kindly greeted the faithful women.
They ran to him and, clasping his knees and feet,
fearfully worshipped Jesus, the conqueror of death.
Then he strengthened their hearts with these instructions:
'Let all fear depart from your faithful minds, and these
commands, see, take quickly to our brothers:
if they long to see me, let them go willingly
and hasten across into the land of Galilee.'
Meanwhile the hearts of the guards at the tomb were terrified;
they sent some of their number to report these great
wonders to the Jews. But that mad band,
now wholly given over once and for all to insane fury,
eagerly paid the soldiers large rewards
and with silver bought a story: that, breaking the entrance,
and shielded by darkness, the daring of the disciples
had stolen the body away, carrying it off in secret.
And now the anxious company of his followers, hastening at Christ's command,
had climbed the mountains of Galilee:
see, the venerable offspring of the Thunderer is seen by his own.
The whole band fell down and devoutly worshipped him;
yet strength did not remain equally firm
in every heart, for some of them doubted.
Then Jesus in his glory addressed the disciples thus:
'In heaven and on earth my Father has subjected all things to me;
the Father deigned to send me to you as light.
In just the same way I have now resolved to send you to all nations;
it is your task to join all nations to me.
Go, and wash men clean in purifying waters,
in the holy name of the Father and the Son,
and let the breath of the life-giving Spirit flow with them.
Then teach those who have been washed my
precepts, so that they may lead everlasting life;
and my presence will never be lacking to you
until the consuming end dissolves the ages.'
My mind has taken hold of this strength of faith and holy fear,
and the grace of Christ shines on me so brightly
that in my verses the glory of the divine law
has gladly put on the earthly ornaments of language.
This the peace of Christ has granted me, this the peace of our age,
which the gracious ruler of the wide earth fosters,
Constantine, on whom rests the favour his merits deserve,
who alone of kings dreads to have the weight of the sacred name
laid upon himself, so that, made worthier by his just deeds,
he may gain eternal life through the divine ages
through Christ, the Lord of light, who reigns for ever.
